06What the deferred frame stores at a visible surface

A map of the complete frame

The map names four shared inputs: A is the camera's stored surface interaction, B is the geometry available to secondary rays, C is cached outgoing surface radiance, and H is retained state. The three primary-view branches answer different parts of the same rendering equation: explicit direct-light connections, the remaining diffuse field, and the remaining glossy field. Their contributions meet in scene-linear composition before display processing.

Two boundaries matter here. Primary VSM projection supplies shadow visibility for deferred direct-light BRDF evaluation, while card direct lighting has its own secondary-surface shadow queries. The captured card schedule also combines lighting both before and after radiosity. The first combine exposes fresh direct illumination and retained indirect illumination to the radiosity traces; the second incorporates their newly integrated indirect result. Neither the cache diagram nor its feedback arrow means that every frame advances exactly one light bounce.

The captured invocation shows how dependency and timing differ. Card lighting and both combines occur before the base pass, while screen-probe integration and reflection reconstruction occur before the recorded primary VSM projection and deferred sun-light pass. The later diffuse-indirect composition consumes their results. The captured-frame explorer and evidence keep the individual passes and bindings; the map gives the system-level reading order.

The yellow branch leads to the dedicated Direct lighting chapter; the blue glossy branch leads to Reflections. Those chapters cover each branch's inputs, sampling, intermediate state, and contribution to the final image.

Build a dependable first interaction before adding a global-illumination cache. A camera path tracer finds that interaction by tracing a ray; a deferred renderer rasterizes visible triangles into depth and material records. At a covered pixel, both methods try to identify the surface the camera sees. Rasterization amortizes this work over coherent screen samples, so many lighting operations reuse the result.

Construct and decode the GBuffer

A minimal implementation stores depth, a shading normal, diffuse or base color, roughness, metallic, specular or F₀ information, a shading-model identity, and velocity for later reprojection. Depending on the platform and shader permutation, the base pass can accumulate emissive output directly into SceneColor. Decode channels using the producer’s layout. Screenshot colors depend on the display mapping.

Material evaluation runs before the GBuffer write. Vertex attributes and interpolated texture coordinates enter the compiled material program; texture samples, constants, and graph operations produce material properties, and tangent-space normals are transformed into the shading frame. Opaque coverage is selected with the depth test. Masked geometry must apply its opacity decision in every representation that needs consistent visibility. Texture normalization, sRGB decoding, tangent handedness, normal normalization and roughness remapping all affect the computed result.

Depth usually starts in device coordinates. Convert it before interpreting a difference in metres. Reconstruct the point with the appropriate inverse view-projection transform and homogeneous divide. In Unreal, reversed depth, translated-world coordinates, view-rectangle offsets, temporal jitter, and large-world origins all affect the result. In schematic form:

uv = (pixel + sample_offset - view_rect_min) / view_rect_size
clip = make_clip_position(uv, device_depth, projection_convention)
position_h = inverse_view_projection * clip
position = position_h.xyz / position_h.w
normal = decode_and_normalize_gbuffer_normal(pixel)
material = decode_material(pixel, shading_model_id)
outgoing = normalize(camera_position - position)

A half-resolution lighting buffer must map back through the correct full-resolution view rectangle. A shifted depth lookup can look like bad GI at edges when the real problem is addressing. The reference's decoded GBuffer records preserve the actual channel layout and pixel arithmetic of the instrumented room frame.

Decode three actual Sponza interactions

Return to A and B on the foreground floor and C on the polished gold sphere. These images decode the final scene invocation of one captured GPU frame, using its 1280 × 720 view rectangle. The backing textures are 1280 × 888, so the unused bottom rows are excluded. The four pictures ask different questions about the same interaction.

The normal image maps each normalized component with 32 + round(223(N/2 + 1/2)), and roughness uses 32 + round(223r). Black is reserved for invalid pixels, which distinguishes missing geometry from a valid zero channel. BaseColor is decoded to linear RGB and displayed with the sRGB transfer function, with code 0 reserved for invalid pixels. Each view uses the data display described in its caption. The figure manifest records every mapping and range, including separate metallic and validity images.

For example, C's GBufferC memory bytes are (157,227,255,255), so the RGB codes are (255,227,157), which decode to the linear gold color above. The two floor points are different texture samples: their color and normal differences must remain in any numerical lighting comparison.

The full receiver record retains all sampled bytes, packed words, material channels, neighboring-pixel checks, formats, row pitches, hashes, and producing/consuming versions. GBufferA/B/C/D were written at pass 697, GBufferF at 700, and the direct-light consumer is pass 842; the consumed GBuffer and depth copies are byte-identical to the recorded producers. The view record gives the inverse transforms and both independent world-position reconstructions. Unreal's depth linearization yields centimetres in this scene; divide by 100 for the metre values above. The view's PreExposure is 1/2048, while these material and geometric channels have no exposure factor.

Read the material before the light. Pick courtyard stone and the metallic test sphere. Both may look bright in the base-color view. They should differ in the metallic view; the polished sphere should be low in the roughness view, and its smooth normal gradient should differ from the stone's mapped detail. If these inputs are wrong, changing Lumen's ray budget cannot produce the intended reflection.

07Direct lighting and the shadows each light casts

Start at courtyard point A. A direct connection joins the light to A and then A to the camera, without another scattering surface between the light and A. The GBuffer already supplies A's position, normal, material, and outgoing camera direction. Direct lighting adds the other half: which lights reach A, how much incident energy they supply, whether geometry blocks them, and how A scatters that energy toward the camera.

A direct connection says nothing about the BRDF. The same analytic light can produce both a broad diffuse response and a narrow specular highlight. A reflection of a sunlit wall, by contrast, contains a secondary surface interaction and belongs to the scene-reflection path. Without that separation, a direct highlight can be added once by deferred lighting and again by an overlapping reflection estimate.

Turn each light type into an incident-light query

For each relevant analytic light, determine its direction or finite-source distribution, radiometric scale, attenuation and support, visibility, and the material response. The point-light ideal is proportional to intensity divided by squared distance. Engine attenuation also includes finite influence and source-shape conventions. A finite rectangle subtends an angular region; evaluating it requires an integral or an approximation such as the engine's area-light treatment. A finite emitter can share a point light’s center and still cover a range of directions at the receiver.

For ideal point and directional lights, let Eℓ⊥(x)E_\ell^\perp(x)Eℓ⊥​(x) denote the incident irradiance on a plane perpendicular to the light direction at x. For a point source of radiant intensity IℓI_\ellIℓ​, it is Iℓ/r2I_\ell/r^2Iℓ​/r2. For an ideal directional source, it stays constant with receiver distance. With the common geometric/shading normal n used in our first model, the owned direct contribution is

Ldirect(x,ωo)=∑ℓ∈LDfs(x;ωℓ ⁣→ ⁣ωo) Eℓ⊥(x) max⁡(0,n⋅ωℓ) Vℓ(x).L_{\rm direct}(x,\omega_o)=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal L_D} f_s(x;\omega_\ell\!\to\!\omega_o)\, E_\ell^\perp(x)\,\max(0,n\cdot\omega_\ell)\,V_\ell(x).Ldirect​(x,ωo​)=ℓ∈LD​∑​fs​(x;ωℓ​→ωo​)Eℓ⊥​(x)max(0,n⋅ωℓ​)Vℓ​(x).
LaTeX source
L_{\rm direct}(x,\omega_o)=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal L_D}
f_s(x;\omega_\ell\!\to\!\omega_o)\,
E_\ell^\perp(x)\,\max(0,n\cdot\omega_\ell)\,V_\ell(x).

Use the directional delta source’s integrated weight in this expression. A spotlight additionally restricts the angular support and varies intensity within its cone. A production local light also has a finite influence bound and source-shape parameters. A finite area source returns to the area/solid-angle integral derived earlier: different source points can have different directions, distances, BRDF values, and visibility. Replacing that integral with one center sample changes the target, especially near large sources.

Check the multiplication before building the shadow system. Give a Lambertian receiver reflectance 0.6 and zero emission. Let one prescribed light supply perpendicular irradiance 10 W m⁻², with incident cosine 0.5 and visibility estimate 0.75. The irradiance reaching the surface is 10 × 0.5 × 0.75 = 3.75 W m⁻². Its outgoing diffuse radiance is (0.6/π) × 3.75 ≈ 0.7162 W m⁻² sr⁻¹. A specular material adds the corresponding specular-BRDF response to this same owned source. This analytic example tests units and factor placement; the Sponza values below use Unreal's recorded RGB calibration.

Evaluate the material at the receiver

A basic direct-light implementation can start with point and directional lights, exact shadow rays, and the diffuse-plus-GGX BSDF already derived. Then replace only the visibility query with a shadow-map query. That gives a controlled before/after test: the BSDF and source stay fixed while the visibility representation changes. Tiled or clustered light lists avoid evaluating every scene light at every pixel. These lists are culling structures, so a false negative loses illumination; a conservative false positive merely costs work.

for light_id in lights_overlapping_pixel_or_cluster:
    light = decode_light(light_id)
    incident = evaluate_light_geometry_and_radiance(light, position)
    visibility = evaluate_shadow(light, position, normal)
    brdf = evaluate_diffuse_plus_specular(material, incident.wi, outgoing)
    scene_color += brdf * incident.radiometric_factor * visibility

The factor in this pseudocode includes the incident cosine and whichever source integration convention the chosen light uses. Check the function’s return convention. Some production functions already include part of the lighting integral. Its units and cosine placement must be documented before multiplying it by another helper.

In a deferred implementation, decode the shading-model identity before interpreting its material payload. A Default Lit metal uses its base color primarily as colored specular reflectance; a dielectric retains a diffuse color and its interface reflectance. Compute the light/view half-vector and the selected distribution, visibility, and Fresnel terms in the same normalized shading frame. The source may fold the microfacet denominator into a visibility helper and may integrate a finite source analytically. Multiplying a textbook GGX denominator around that helper a second time is a different BRDF. The earlier microfacet derivation supplies the target; the selected shader supplies its implementation convention.

Light culling and light evaluation are also separate. A light volume, screen rectangle, tile list, or cluster list decides which receivers might be affected. Attenuation, cone support, lighting channels, light functions, and shadowing decide the contribution after that conservative selection. The captured Sponza sun uses a standard deferred light pass. The loop illustrates who computes each term. The captured sun’s actual dispatch is identified separately.

Follow that multiplication in the captured legacy GBuffer route: the deferred lighting accumulator computes local attenuation, obtains the applicable shadow terms, calls IntegrateBxDF for the selected source shape, applies the light's diffuse/specular scales, and accumulates the split result with attenuated light color and surface shadow. That helper's source integration is already part of the returned lighting. The example capture has Substrate disabled; other material permutations require their own decode and integration contracts.

Construct the shadow views from the light

We know which surface the camera sees. Shadowing asks a different visibility question: what lies between that surface and a particular light? A shadow map answers by rasterizing the scene from a light-dependent view. Its texels store the nearest represented blocker along that view's rays. The primary camera identifies the receivers. The shadow pass renders depth from the light’s projection.

How a directional light covers the scene

An ideal directional light supplies parallel incident rays. Build an orthonormal light-space frame with two transverse axes a and b and a depth axis. In a teaching orthographic view centered at c, with transverse half-width R, a world point x maps to

u=12+a⋅(x−c)2R,v=12−b⋅(x−c)2R.u=\frac12+\frac{a\cdot(x-c)}{2R},\qquad v=\frac12-\frac{b\cdot(x-c)}{2R}.u=21​+2Ra⋅(x−c)​,v=21​−2Rb⋅(x−c)​.
LaTeX source
u=\frac12+\frac{a\cdot(x-c)}{2R},\qquad
v=\frac12-\frac{b\cdot(x-c)}{2R}.

The sign on v is a chosen texture-coordinate convention. Unlike perspective projection, there is no division by distance along the light ray. In the sun’s orthographic projection, moving a column along the light-view axis preserves its projected size. We still need a finite depth interval that includes relevant casters, a world-to-light transform, and a finite transverse region to store.

One enormous orthographic map would spend the same texel density everywhere. Directional VSM clipmaps instead provide nested light-space coverage around the view, with increasing world-space footprint at coarser levels. A receiver selects a suitable level; virtual pages provide sparse storage within that level. Clipmap level and texture mip level are different indices. In the captured sun, IDs 8192–8208 represent clip levels 6–22; the storage example below uses ID 8196, clip level 10, at logical mip 0.

A stable light-space grid matters as much as resolution, because reuse depends on it. If the grid followed every subtexel camera translation continuously, the same stationary edge would move across depth texels every frame. Snapping the clipmap to that grid and maintaining it makes reuse possible. When coverage scrolls, the system can retain overlapping world regions and request newly exposed pages, provided the represented light transform, depth range, and validity state remain compatible.

The actual clipmap placement snaps the light-space center to a level-dependent grid. The reversed-Z orthographic matrix sets its transverse extent and depth range, while receiver level selection begins with the logarithm of distance from the clipmap origin. The policy changes spatial resolution while keeping the sun direction fixed.

Local lights need perspective directions and a finite influence bound

For a local source at o, let q = x − o and d be its component along a selected shadow face's forward axis. If θ is that face's horizontal half-angle, its horizontal coordinate in a symmetric perspective view is

u=12+a⋅q2dtan⁡θ.u=\frac12+\frac{a\cdot q}{2d\tan\theta}.u=21​+2dtanθa⋅q​.
LaTeX source
u=\frac12+\frac{a\cdot q}{2d\tan\theta}.

The vertical coordinate has the corresponding vertical half-angle and texture-axis sign. This division by d is what lets rays diverge from a point. A spot light uses its orientation and outer cone to choose a perspective frustum. Its attenuation radius bounds how far the implementation searches and casts; the outer cone bounds angular support. The inner cone controls light intensity. The shadow view has its own coverage boundary.

A point light illuminates directions around its position. Six perspective views, facing ±X, ±Y and ±Z, cover those directions as cube faces. Each face has its own virtual-page region and projection. The selected direction determines the face; a point close to a face boundary needs consistent face selection and filtering, or the shadow develops seams. The light's influence radius also limits the caster and receiver region. The renderer truncates the light’s influence at this radius. An ideal inverse-square field would continue beyond it.

The pinned engine's rectangular-light whole-scene shadow initializer also selects the one-pass point-light/cubemap route. The direct-light evaluation still uses the rectangular emitter’s finite shape. Its VSM soft-shadow path approximates that shape separately. The stored visibility representation is therefore built from that selected set of projection views. A true area-light visibility integral would ask for visibility from many different emitter positions. VSM reuses the stored depth representation to estimate visibility at multiple points on the emitter.

That approximation is concrete in this version: the rect light supplies half its width as SourceRadius and half its height as SourceLength. The inspected local VSM ray generator samples a disk using SourceRadius. The rectangle’s two dimensions belong to the direct-light evaluation. Thus the stored cube depth and the disk-based soft-shadow estimate are each approximations, separate from the rectangle used by the direct-light BRDF integral. Follow the rect shadow initializer, rect source parameters, and local SMRT ray generator. A separate ray-traced area-shadow implementation can use a different sampling rule.

The local-light implementations make the bounds concrete: the spot initializer uses inverse tangent of the outer cone, while point and rectangular initializers select the cubemap path. All three retain a near limit and a maximum casting distance. These parameters belong in the projection record alongside the light identity; they cannot be inferred from a depth texture's width and height. The spot initializer supplies the cone scale; the six-face setup supplies face directions, up vectors, and a 90-degree perspective matrix with near depth 1 and far depth equal to the light radius. Those are the actual cube-projection values, even though the earlier initializer also carries its own minimum-light-depth field.

Rasterize casters into the requested depth pages

Start with an ordinary nonvirtual shadow map. For each eligible caster triangle, apply its current object deformation and transform, then the light-view and projection matrices. Clip against the light frustum, rasterize the projected triangle, and evaluate any required masked-material coverage. At each covered depth texel, retain the nearest blocker in the chosen depth convention. The image stores depth. Material albedo and shaded color enter other passes. Material coverage and vertex motion can still change which fragments reach it.

Let d be positive forward depth in a perspective shadow view with near and far depths denoted by the subscripts “near” and “far”. A reversed-Z teaching projection has the form A + B/d. Requiring the near plane to map to 1 and the far plane to 0 gives

z(d)=dneardfar(dfar−dnear)d−dneardfar−dnear.z(d)=\frac{d_{\rm near}d_{\rm far}}{(d_{\rm far}-d_{\rm near})d}-\frac{d_{\rm near}}{d_{\rm far}-d_{\rm near}}.z(d)=(dfar​−dnear​)ddnear​dfar​​−dfar​−dnear​dnear​​.
LaTeX source
z(d)=\frac{d_{\rm near}d_{\rm far}}{(d_{\rm far}-d_{\rm near})d}-\frac{d_{\rm near}}{d_{\rm far}-d_{\rm near}}.

For an orthographic view the corresponding mapping is linear, z(d) = (far − d)/(far − near). These formulas convert projection depth. Closer blockers have larger z under this convention. A clear value of zero represents the far end of an otherwise valid empty depth image. With a positive floating-point depth encoding, unsigned integer ordering preserves the order of those depth values; this lets the virtual-depth raster path use an integer maximum operation on their bit patterns. The sampling path later reinterprets the word as a float.

Now virtualize the same operation. Receivers mark needed light-space pages and resolution levels. Allocation supplies physical tiles and their state. Caster culling determines which scene instances and triangles overlap those requested page frusta. The raster path translates each covered virtual texel to its physical tile and writes depth there. Nanite and conventional geometry have different submission, culling, and raster implementations, but both must satisfy the same address, depth, and validity contract before projection samples the result. In the conventional VSM depth pixel shader, a decoded page must have rendering validity before InterlockedMax writes asuint(DeviceZ) to the translated address. The static-page bit chooses the static cache slice; other depth goes to slice zero.

For an ideal single depth comparison at receiver x, a simple reversed-Z visibility estimate is

V~(x)=1 ⁣[zs(u(x),v(x))≤zr(x)+ϵ(x)].\widetilde V(x)=\mathbf 1\!\left[z_s(u(x),v(x))\le z_r(x)+\epsilon(x)\right].V(x)=1[zs​(u(x),v(x))≤zr​(x)+ϵ(x)].
LaTeX source
\widetilde V(x)=\mathbf 1\!\left[z_s(u(x),v(x))\le z_r(x)+\epsilon(x)\right].

Here zₛ is the stored blocker depth, zᵣ is the receiver depth in the same projection, and ε represents a declared comparison bias in these depth units. A positive bias makes this simple test more permissive. The production path has receiver-normal, slope, footprint, and soft-shadow rules that must be followed in their own units and order. Increasing ε arbitrarily can hide acne by detaching shadows and admitting light through thin blockers.

A finite source produces partial visibility because different source points can be blocked differently. Filtering a depth representation is therefore an approximation to a visibility integral. SMRT walks selected rays through shadow-map depths to estimate that soft visibility. Each texel stores only the nearest depth. All filter samples drawn from that layer lack the occluders hidden behind it. The captured mask records the visibility computed from those samples.

Moving lights change the meaning of cached depth

Imagine moving a point light sideways while leaving every wall fixed. The same wall projects to different cube-face texels, and its depth changes relative to the new light origin. Keeping the old depth pages and merely replacing the light matrix would compare new receiver coordinates against old caster coordinates. A moved local light therefore requires compatible cache invalidation and refreshed shadow views. Rotating a directional light similarly changes the light-space projection of the entire scene. The pinned cache keys contain WorldToLight, PreShadowTranslation, and distant-light status for a local light, and light direction plus first level for a directional clipmap. Changing a key invalidates the rendered-frame state; the subsequent uncached render establishes reusable contents.

Moving only the primary camera is a different operation. It changes visible receiver demand and directional-clipmap coverage, while a stationary light and stationary caster can still describe the same world-space depth in overlapping valid pages. A moving caster instead invalidates the pages intersected by its old/new affected bounds. Deformation, world-position offset, masked coverage changes, and changes to shadow-casting participation also belong in the invalidation policy. Updating an object's transform without updating its shadow dependencies leaves an apparently stable but stale cache. The implementation projects affected instance bounds into allocated pages and sets invalidation flags there. During camera motion, clipmap reuse retains the cached depth interval and records a page-address offset while the depth guard band and other validity tests pass. A failed test invalidates the level.

Separate static and dynamic depth storage can preserve static geometry while dynamic geometry is cleared and rendered again, then combine the required depths for sampling. Here the static/dynamic merge takes the maximum of the two stored reversed-Z words, so the nearer represented blocker wins; the merge is dispatched for pages selected by the corresponding dirty-state path. A physical allocation, an initialized tile, a cacheable tile, and a tile whose contents are valid for the current projection are distinct states. The storage section below decodes those records independently. Its request counter uses scene-frame numbering. Use the screen-probe history’s own counter or each capture’s own frame number when examining those records.

Changing only a light’s intensity or color leaves the ideal shadow geometry in place. It changes the lighting multiplied by visibility. A cache key can encode that distinction, even if a production update path conservatively invalidates more state after a light-proxy change. Position, orientation, shape-dependent projection, influence bounds and caster state can change the depth geometry.

A light or caster can be outside the primary image

First consider an off-screen light. Its source position may project outside the image while its influence volume overlaps visible floor or walls. The renderer must retain it for those receivers. Test the projected influence bound, such as a point-light sphere or spot cone, when culling. It can cover receivers even when the source itself is offscreen. A directional light can illuminate receivers anywhere in view, even with the sun disk offscreen.

Next consider an off-screen caster. A column behind the camera can stand between a visible floor point and a local light. The floor marks a page in the light's projection. Rendering that page must consider eligible geometry in the corresponding light-space caster region, including geometry omitted from the primary camera's color and depth buffers. Raster shadow maps can therefore represent this shadow even though a screen-depth-only trace cannot see the column. Culling casters solely against the primary view would be a correctness error.

Finally consider an off-screen receiver. It creates no primary opaque-pixel demand in this view, but the renderer may need broader/coarser shadow coverage for other consumers, such as translucent lighting and volumetrics. Those consumers have their own request and sampling policies. Fine page requests from visible opaque receivers establish coverage for those receivers. Check offscreen secondary surfaces separately. Card lighting and hit lighting query shadows along their own routes. The primary camera’s mask belongs to the visible receiver at that pixel.

The source keeps receiver and caster work separate: local receiver marking queries the culled light grid at visible depth, then applies radius, cone, and rect-facing tests; local caster culling uses the light's bounds and caster frustum. Directional coarse pages and local coarse pages provide broader coverage for their consumers. This page-marking path has no Lumen-card receiver input. An off-screen blocker can therefore cast a visible shadow, and fine primary-view coverage cannot be assumed for every secondary surface.

Virtual Shadow Maps: spend depth storage where receivers need it

A shadow map looks at geometry from a light and stores the nearest depth. Transform a receiver into the light's projection and compare its depth with the stored depth. If it lies behind the nearest occluder, that light connection is blocked. In Sponza, balcony rails and columns create rapidly changing visibility, so a low-resolution uniform shadow map loses detail while a huge one wastes storage elsewhere.

Virtual Shadow Maps separate a large logical address space from a smaller pool of physical depth pages. Visible receivers mark required pages at appropriate resolution. The system allocates physical pages, reuses valid cached ones, invalidates pages affected by moving geometry or lights, culls geometry into the requested pages, and renders their depth. A lookup translates the virtual address through the page table before reading the physical tile. Directional-light clipmaps supply scale and coverage around the view; local lights use their appropriate projections and mip levels.

Build a minimal virtual implementation in this order: a fixed light-space depth image; a tiled image with an identity page table; receiver-driven page requests; physical allocation with residency/validity bits; cached pages with explicit invalidation; then clipmaps or mips. At every stage compare the resulting visibility against the nonvirtual image. Otherwise allocation errors become indistinguishable from shadow bias errors.

The pinned renderer exposes these handoffs in page marking, allocation, and shadow rendering. After rendering and its page-state updates, the projection entry points distinguish local-light projections from directional clipmaps and composite their visibility masks. Check depth validity after resolving the allocated address.

Depth bias prevents the receiver's own numerical depth error from becoming a false occluder. Too much bias separates shadows from their casters and permits leaks. Filtering approximates the variation of visibility across a footprint or finite source. Unreal's Shadow Map Ray Tracing (SMRT) samples virtual shadow depths along rays used for soft-shadow estimation. The query sees only the occluder layers available in the depth representation. Missing layers, thin geometry, projection boundaries, and finite sample counts explain artifacts that a higher lighting sample count cannot fix. Here VSM stands for Virtual Shadow Maps. Variance Shadow Mapping is a separate technique with the same initials.

Walk a virtual shadow address through allocation and sampling

Use a small teaching shadow image of 1024×1024 texels, split into 128×128 pages. There are 8×8 logical pages. A light-space receiver at uv = (0.31, 0.72) lands at texel (317,737), virtual page (2,5), and local texel (61,97), using floor and a half-open [0,1) image domain. Suppose page (2,5) maps to physical tile (7,3). Its physical address is then (957,481), before any implementation-specific border. Decoding the address requires the projection or light identity and the residency entry.

// A teaching VSM cycle. Production layouts and packing differ.
Mark:       project visible receivers; choose level; atomically mark page requests
Allocate:   keep valid residents; assign free physical tiles to new requests
Invalidate: mark pages touched by changed lights or moving caster bounds
Cull:       find casters overlapping requested dirty page frusta
Render:     clear new/dirty page depth, then rasterize nearest occluder depth
Sample:     translate light/level/page through the page table; compare depths

Rendering must happen before a newly allocated page becomes sampleable. A resident page can be dirty. Check its state before using its contents for this light. A finite memory pool also needs a defined overflow policy. When a page is unmapped, report the condition and take the defined fallback. Keep request count, allocation count, cached reuse count, dirty count, and overflow count visible during development.

For a conventional depth that increases away from the light, a minimal comparison is visible if receiverDepth ≤ storedDepth + bias. Reverse the ordering when the actual stored depth convention reverses it. For a finite area source, the ideal direct estimate integrates visibility over source points. Filtering and SMRT approximate that varying visibility using the depth representation and finite samples. Occluders hidden behind the stored depth can still lie on a source-to-receiver segment.

Read the storage before interpreting the shadow

A shadow mask is the answer to a visibility query. The physical depth pool is one of the data structures used to obtain that answer. Neighboring physical tiles can cover distant parts of Sponza because the allocator uses whichever slots are free. To recover a light-space image, we must follow the page table in the opposite direction, gathering the physical tiles into their virtual locations.

Three separate questions determine what a sample means. Which virtual address did this light projection request? Which physical tile currently backs that address? Which depth values in that tile are valid for this query? The page table answers the second; flags and cache metadata constrain the third. Page-table colors distinguish address categories.

The physical pool is 16,384×4,096 texels, with two captured array slices. Projection samples slice 0; the separately cached static depth uses slice 1 in this configuration. Each slice occupies 256 MiB at four bytes per texel. Free slots provide no shadow answers until a mapping and valid contents back them. The smaller table and metadata let the renderer decide which parts of that memory represent a requested light-space region.

A directional fallback in this table selects a coarser clipmap level, still sampled at logical mip 0. For a local shadow map, the corresponding LOD mechanism can select a coarser logical mip of that map. An address translation must know which policy it is applying. Large regions of the full map above reference the same coarser physical tiles.

Logical shadow mips, hardware texture mips, and hierarchical flags

A full VSM's logical mip 0 has 128×128 page entries. Logical mips 1–7 have 64², 32², 16², 8², 4², 2², and 1² entries. All eight regions fit inside one 128×192 block of the page-table texture's hardware mip 0. Relative to that block, mip 0 begins at (0,0); the tail begins at Y=128, with X offsets 0, 64, 96, 112, 120, 124, and 126 for mips 1–7. The selected map's block begins at global texel (640,0). Thus its logical-mip-zero page (63,65) occupies table texel (703,65).

The logical-level packing is separate from the PageFlags texture's hardware mip pyramid. Each PageFlags word uses the low six bits for allocation, dynamic uncached, static uncached, detail geometry, primary request, and secondary request. The hierarchy update ORs those flags into coarser texture mips at shifted addresses. Each hierarchy level has its own mip address. Eight six-bit levels would require 48 bits if packed together. The hierarchy lets a culling operation ask whether a larger page region contains relevant work without inspecting every leaf.

The page size in this source version is 128×128 texels. For a nonnegative integer virtual texel address u at an already selected level, split each coordinate into a page coordinate p and a local coordinate q:

u=128p+q,p=⌊u/128⌋,q=u mod 128.u=128p+q,\qquad p=\lfloor u/128\rfloor,\qquad q=u\bmod128.u=128p+q,p=⌊u/128⌋,q=umod128.
LaTeX source
u=128p+q,\qquad p=\lfloor u/128\rfloor,\qquad q=u\bmod128.

Read the page-table entry for this shadow-map identity, level, and p. If it supplies a valid physical page coordinate a at this same level, the physical texel address is t = 128a + q. The offset within a page survives the translation; only the page's location changes. A nonzero LOD offset selects a coarser level. Recompute the virtual coordinates for that level before sampling.

The page-entry decoder and texel translation derive “this level valid” from bit 31 being set and the LOD offset being zero. A zero word marks an invalid entry. A valid reference to physical page (0,0) needs its validity bits. Rendering validity and sampling validity are separate predicates. What a physical depth texel actually stores

The projection shader's physical load reads an unsigned 32-bit word from pool layer zero and reinterprets the same bits as floating-point depth. The integer representation supports the renderer's storage and raster operations, while the interpreted floating-point value participates in the light-space depth test.

0.49980.500050.5003

Stored device Z · larger means closer to this light

Every selected-depth view uses the same range, 0.4998…0.5003, with color coordinate t = (z − 0.4998)/0.0005. The 99 native pages contain 1,622,016 depth values, spanning approximately 0.499898583…0.500238657; none is zero. Expanding this narrow numeric interval makes the geometry legible without changing the stored values. Independent per-tile contrast adjustment would destroy this comparison. RGB quantization and thumbnail averaging still lose precision, so use the retained float and raw-word arrays for numerical work.

A's stored depth nearly equals its receiver projection, with a difference of about −1.86×10⁻⁸ before bias. B's stored depth exceeds its receiver depth by about 0.000271428, consistent with a blocker closer to the light in reversed Z. That is a useful storage check against the captured mask values of 1 and 0. One center test illustrates the depth comparison. Replaying SMRT would require the ray directions, jitter, slope and normal handling, and individual sample decisions that the snapshot omits.

A depth value belongs to its light projection and level. It is neither camera depth nor a distance in centimeters by itself. Clear depth inside a valid mapped page and storage in an unallocated page are also different states. The first can mean that no occluder was written at that texel; the second has no usable visibility interpretation. The display gives each category its own color.

Physical-page records and the complete retained operands

Each physical-page metadata record contains six uint32 words: Flags, LastRequestedSceneFrameNumber, VirtualShadowMapId, MipLevel, and the two components of PageAddress. A and B both carry physical flags 0x5b and request number 904. Their independent PageFlags value is 0x1b. In the physical record, 0x40 marks initialized dynamic storage. Address bits use the separate page-table layout.

Follow the shadow result into the direct-light addition

The mask texture stores square-root-encoded attenuation. Decode its red byte c as (c/255)²; treating c/255 as linear would brighten partially shadowed samples. At A the byte is 255 and the consumed attenuation is 1. At B and C it is 0. The sun pass adds pre-exposed RGB (1.9306641, 1.3037109, 0.7900391) at A and exactly (0,0,0) at B and C. Thus the gold sphere can be bright in the final image while receiving no contribution from this analytic sun at that particular point: its reflected incident field belongs to another term of our partition.

The encode/decode functions establish this square-root convention. The mask is a packed set of attenuation channels: the red channel carries this sun's whole-scene directional shadow, while other channels serve subsurface, per-object, or light-function terms in applicable branches. Decode each shadow-mask channel according to the selected light path.

Subtract the captured FP16 SceneColor before pass 842, RenderLight Light::StandardDeferred: Sun_Sponza, from SceneColor after it to obtain these values. Dividing by PreExposure = 1/2048 converts A's addition to scene-linear RGB (3954,2670,1618) in the engine's RGB calibration. Interpret the channels in the renderer’s color and exposure convention. For the image only, each positive pre-exposed channel is mapped through L/(1+L), then the sRGB transfer function. The exact linear values remain in the receiver record.

What this shadow record proves, and what a depth-query replay additionally needs

The mask is the ShadowMaskTexture produced by pass 841 and consumed as PS.LightAttenuationTexture at 842. Its B and A memory channels remain clear; R and G agree on valid geometry in this capture. The observed red codes are 0,90,127,156,180,202,221,239,255, approximately the square roots of eighth-step visibility after quantization. The record reports the quantized value actually available.

This proves the mask-to-direct-light boundary. Reconstructing how the mask was generated would require its SMRT ray samples, virtual-page lookups, receiver bias and depth comparisons. The full frame package retains the VSM page tables, physical pool, projection data, parameters, and captured versions for inspection; the source-level lookup algorithm is explained above and in the VSM reference. An exact per-thread SMRT replay would need additional instrumentation to record the random choices and shader-local operands. A declared replay over these resources must identify its selected samples separately from captured execution.

The direct-light path replaces exact geometric visibility V and some finite-source integration with an estimate V~\widetilde VV and its sampling/filtering rules. The GBuffer provides the primary BSDF. Deferred direct lighting already accounts for this analytic contribution at the visible pixel. It does need direct illumination on secondary surfaces, because those surfaces become sources of reflected radiance for other points.

Implementation checkpoints and exact source reference

The existing VSM implementation reference follows page marking, allocation, invalidation, depth rendering, SMRT, and physical-pool decoding in the pinned source. It also records why a raw pool image cannot be interpreted without virtual-to-physical mappings. The material reference separates the legacy GBuffer route from Substrate and documents the compile-time permutations. These layouts apply to the selected capture. Check the producer’s layout in each project.

08Tracing geometry outside the camera view

An incoming-light query begins in the shaded arcade and follows a sampled direction. It may hit a column, pass into the courtyard, or miss toward the sky. Tracing every query against full triangle geometry is expensive. The depth buffer already holds detailed visible surfaces, including the rasterized material geometry, so begin there.

First try screen depth, but define what a hit proves

Project points along the ray into screen space and compare the ray's depth with scene depth. A hierarchy of depth bounds lets traversal skip large screen regions when no intersection is possible and descend near a candidate crossing. The resulting hierarchical Z buffer (HZB) stores min/max or conservative bounds, depending on its depth convention. With reversed depth, the intuitive meaning of "larger" flips. The comparison must follow the actual producer.

Validate a depth crossing against the hit criteria before accepting it. The screen records the frontmost visible surface at each pixel. Its thickness and hidden layers have to come from elsewhere. A thickness test determines whether the crossing is plausibly near the represented surface. Edge uncertainty, missing back layers, view boundaries, and unsupported materials can require rejection. If accepted, the shader must obtain a suitable lighting value at the hit; it cannot sample arbitrary tone-mapped final color without changing the transport quantity and risking feedback.

result = trace_hzb(ray, depth_pyramid, thickness_rule)
if result.accepted:
    radiance = sample_valid_screen_lighting(result)
else:
    append_unresolved_ray(origin, direction, distance_interval,
                          receiver_id, sample_id, pdf, trace_flags)

The output record must carry the state later stages depend on. A compacted queue needs the original receiver/sample mapping so the result lands in the right directional cell. Keep validity separate from radiance so a valid hit on a black wall survives decoding. The remaining distance interval and any bias must match how the next tracing stage interprets the origin.

Make traversal and fallback independently testable

Begin with a slow screen-space ray marcher at full-resolution depth. Transform the origin and direction into view space, clip the segment to the valid near plane and screen rectangle, and step through projected pixels. Use perspective-correct interpolation to evaluate the projected world-space ray’s depth along the screen trace. Compare a conservative ray-depth interval against the represented surface-depth interval. Refine a candidate crossing before accepting it.

Then add the hierarchy. Each coarse HZB texel bounds the depths of its children according to the producer's convention. At a level, advance to the next projected cell boundary when the whole ray interval is safely in front of the represented bound. Descend when a crossing is possible. At the finest level, apply the thickness and hit-validity rules. Limit both the distance and iteration count. On leaving the view, exhausting its steps or finding an ambiguous crossing, the trace returns unresolved work.

Test the optimized result against the slow marcher on a plane, a thin column, a staircase silhouette, and a ray leaving the screen. Then test both against actual world intersections. The first comparison finds traversal bugs; the second measures the representation's missing information.

For world fallback, prefix-scan the unresolved flags into a compact list and preserve the original result address. Suppose rays 0,2,7 are unresolved: queue slots 0,1,2 must still write back to results 0,2,7. Keep hit distance, hit validity, and radiance validity separate. A valid black surface hit is useful geometric evidence even when its radiance is zero. Resetting all three to zero erases the distinction between an unlit wall and missing representation.

Represent world geometry with distance fields

A signed distance field approximates distance to a surface. For a point outside the surface, an exact field reports distance d to the nearest surface, so a ray can safely advance by d without crossing anything. Repeatedly sample and advance until near zero, beyond the maximum distance, or over the iteration budget. This is sphere tracing.

Mesh distance fields preserve local object detail, while a global distance field combines scene objects into clipmapped volumes with coarser coverage farther from the camera. A practical query can use detailed object fields near the origin and global fields for longer distances. Transform positions and distances consistently under object scale. Handle the inside/outside sign, two-sided meshes, thin surfaces, grid interpolation, and clipmap transitions. A missing or severely compressed wall in this representation can leak light even when rasterization shows the wall perfectly.

Implement a distance-field step without mixing coordinate systems

Store the field's local bounds, world-to-local transform, voxel dimensions, distance scale/bias, and validity. Transform a world sample into local coordinates, map it into the volume's texel domain, interpolate the encoded value, then decode its distance units. If the object has uniform world scale s, a local distance d becomes sd. For a nonuniform scale, multiplying a positive local distance by the smallest singular value of the local-to-world linear transform gives a conservative lower bound on world distance. Multiplying by the largest axis scale can step through a surface.

t = minimum_trace_distance
while t < maximum_trace_distance and steps < maximum_steps:
    x = origin + t * direction
    sample = read_valid_distance_field(x)
    if sample is unavailable: return unresolved
    d = decode_distance_in_world_units(sample)
    if d <= surface_tolerance: return candidate_hit(t)
    step = conservative_step(d, field_error_bound, footprint)
    if step cannot make reliable progress: return unresolved
    t += step
return miss_if_coverage_and_distance_are_complete_else_unresolved

An exact signed distance outside a closed surface supplies a safe step. A filtered, quantized voxel field is approximate: if a proven absolute error bound is ε, max(d−ε,0) is a conservative positive distance bound. Production fields instead use particular expansion, step-factor, minimum-step and tolerance rules. A minimum step can speed progress at the cost of stepping across geometry. A two-sided sheet can report distance on either side while leaving the inside/outside classification of a closed solid undefined.

Build the first version with one object, then compare it against triangle intersections for rays near edges and under scaled transforms. Add object bounds to avoid sampling unrelated volumes. A global union field can use the minimum distance of contributing objects, but a finite clipmap covers only a bounded region. When a ray leaves coverage, continue in another representation or mark it unresolved.

A global-field hit supplies a location and an estimated normal. Identifying the triangle or material would require another lookup. The inspected Lumen path therefore consults a separate page object grid. It offsets the lookup position using the field normal, resolves the global-field page, decodes candidate GPU Scene instance indices, maps each instance to a mesh-card set, and accumulates compatible card samples. The page object grid is a separate data structure from the distance texture. A field can show an occluding wall while its lighting lookup has no valid mesh-card identity. See the field-hit to card-lookup bridge. The Surface Cache chapter follows the remaining address translation.

In Sponza, a column, a cloth sheet, and a thick masonry wall cannot be expected to survive a coarse field equally well. The mesh must be split and built so that useful cards and distance fields exist for its geometry. Importing the whole atrium as one enormous mesh can give a recognizable camera image while making secondary tracing and surface coverage poor.

Hardware tracing improves intersections, while shading stays a separate choice

Hardware ray tracing traverses acceleration structures built from supported geometry. Its hit can be more faithful than a distance-field hit, especially for detailed meshes, but the result still needs shading. One mode shades the hit through the Surface Cache. Another evaluates more of the hit material and direct lighting. The first can combine exact triangle visibility with approximate diffuse cached radiance. Hardware ray tracing accelerates the intersection query. Lumen still uses the lighting and reconstruction stages described here.

Geometry representation choices remain: Nanite fallback geometry versus supported native tracing, skinned updates, masked opacity, instance transforms, material hit groups, and tracing bounds. Keep intersection quality and shading quality as two independent switches in experiments.

For world-tracing continuation, compaction gives the GPU a dense list of selected unresolved rays. A prefix sum or atomic allocator assigns output slots; indirect dispatch dimensions then depend on the remaining count. This avoids repeating the world trace for already-resolved rays. Other queues use other predicates: the reflection chapter also compacts hits that still need lighting. A correct implementation also handles empty dispatches, maximum queue capacity, overflow policy, resource transitions, and synchronization. Asynchronous compute can overlap independent tasks; it cannot let a consumer read an unfinished producer.

These are identical 470×500 source-pixel crops starting at (110, 200), at fixed exposure. The second view disables both r.Lumen.ScreenProbeGather.ScreenTraces and r.Lumen.Reflections.ScreenTraces. The third restores those routes and sets the master r.Lumen.HardwareRayTracing=0. The capture record retains the requested and observed settings and the restoration between cases. This scene shows how the available representation affects the result. Software-traced brightness depends on scene geometry and cached lighting. Trace the difference through the distance fields, card coverage and returned lighting while holding exposure fixed.

A diagnostic that separates representations. Hold the Sponza camera fixed and disable screen traces. Differences reveal what the world-space tracing and hit-lighting representation supplied without screen assistance. Then compare software and hardware tracing while keeping hit-lighting mode fixed. Finally change hit lighting while keeping hardware intersections fixed. Each experiment changes one variable; changing all three together cannot identify the cause of a reflection error.

Once a ray query returns a hit, the next cost is evaluating the radiance leaving that point. The Surface Cache exists to make that evaluation reusable.

Trace state, packed fields, and source details

The tracing implementation reference gives HZB traversal and fallback source locations. The captured distance-field replay decodes one real march, including clipmap/page addressing and stored-format values, before the radiance-cache lookup. These records come from the controlled room experiment.

09Shade a secondary surface once, then reuse it

Suppose thousands of queries from Sponza's shaded arcade hit the same sunlit wall. Tracing each ray already costs work, and evaluating the wall material and its illumination independently at every hit repeats another large computation. A reusable material-and-lighting representation on the wall lets a ray hit answer "what radiance leaves this part of the wall?" with a lookup.

For a diffuse wall, outgoing radiance is independent of outgoing direction, so one RGB value per surface location replaces a complete function over outgoing directions. On a glossy wall, outgoing radiance also depends strongly on viewing direction. The cache's effective fully rough response is an approximation, and its limitations matter for reflections.

Choose a surface parameterization

A traditional texture uses authored UVs. Lumen instead builds a set of oriented cards that capture the mesh from useful directions. The offline mesh-card builder samples visible surfaces from axis-oriented views, creates surfels, rejects unsuitable interior samples, clusters coverage into rectangles, and limits the card budget. At runtime, mesh instances transform this representation into the scene. Merged instances and heightfields have additional paths.

Several cards are needed because a single projection of a column cannot represent all of its sides, and a projection of the whole atrium hides its arcade interiors behind the outer surfaces. Separate meshes and sufficient card coverage give the cache addressable surfaces where rays actually hit. Magenta in the coverage view marks a surface the cache failed to represent.

Start a small implementation with one known rectangular wall and one orthographic capture. Store its world-to-card transform, oriented bounds, normal, and texel scale. Once world positions map reliably to capture pixels, add six possible projection directions, coverage selection, and per-mesh card sets. Test capture depth to distinguish overlapping layers at the same projected coordinates.

Separate logical surface resolution from physical memory

A distant wall can use a coarser cache resolution than a nearby one. Each card therefore needs a logical resolution and page coordinates independent of its current physical atlas placement. A virtual page table maps these coordinates into a finite physical page pool. It also needs enough state to distinguish unmapped, allocated-but-uninitialized, and valid captured data. Sampling stale memory after eviction can look like lighting from an unrelated object.

card_position = world_to_card * hit_position
uv = card_position.xy / card_extent.xy * 0.5 + 0.5
virtual_texel = uv * virtual_resolution
page_xy = floor(virtual_texel / page_payload_size)
within_page = virtual_texel - page_xy * page_payload_size
entry = page_table[card_id, mip, page_xy]
if not entry.resident or not entry.capture_valid: return unsupported
atlas_texel = entry.physical_origin + border + within_page
if not capture_depth_matches_hit(atlas_texel, card_position.z): return unsupported
return sample_final_lighting(atlas_texel, footprint)

The pseudocode is a minimal address contract; Unreal's packed helpers also handle card selection, neighboring contributions, mip/border filtering, virtual-to-physical scale/bias, and depth/normal weighting. The captured texel replay exposes those actual mappings and packed values for one recorded query. The pseudocode above is a simplified lookup contract; use the replay for the packed layout.

Page scheduling needs requests, priority, a work budget, and eviction. A useful priority considers projected importance, distance, lighting changes, and age. Updating everything removes temporal staleness but exceeds the budget; updating only what was visible last frame misses newly revealed surfaces. Material, geometry, and lighting changes have different consequences: a changed material can require recapture, while a moving light may require lighting updates on otherwise valid material pages.

To watch this system over time, track three separate objects. The card bounds describe which part of the mesh can be captured; the page mapping describes where a requested resolution resides; the lighting values describe the most recent estimate stored there. A static wall’s card can stay in place as the camera moves. Its requested resolution and residency can change. A change in sunlight can leave the card and page allocation intact while making the stored lighting stale. A static rectangle can still belong to an actively updating cache. Conversely, a rectangle moving across the screen may only reflect camera motion.

Capture material properties before caching illumination

Render the selected card views into depth and material atlases. The card capture renders the material program from its own viewpoints. Cache capture resolution, normal maps, alpha masks, texture filtering, and view-dependent material logic can therefore produce different results from the primary view. The capture folds a fully rough specular approximation into effective albedo, which can make it differ from the material’s diffuse base color.

The units differ: effective albedo is dimensionless; emissive radiance has radiance units; direct and indirect irradiance have irradiance units; final lighting represents diffuse outgoing radiance. The audited combine operation is

L~card(y)=Le,card(y)+ρeff(y)π[E~direct(y)+E~indirect(y)].\widetilde L_{\rm card}(y)=L_{e,\rm card}(y)+\frac{\rho_{\rm eff}(y)}{\pi} \left[\widetilde E_{\rm direct}(y)+\widetilde E_{\rm indirect}(y)\right].Lcard​(y)=Le,card​(y)+πρeff​(y)​[Edirect​(y)+Eindirect​(y)].
LaTeX source
\widetilde L_{\rm card}(y)=L_{e,\rm card}(y)+\frac{\rho_{\rm eff}(y)}{\pi}
\left[\widetilde E_{\rm direct}(y)+\widetilde E_{\rm indirect}(y)\right].

With effective albedo (0.6,0.3,0.1), zero emission, and total irradiance (10,10,10), the outgoing radiance is approximately (1.910,0.955,0.318). A secondary ray returns that colored radiance, and the receiver later applies its own material. Multiplying by the wall's albedo again at lookup would darken it twice.

The atlases store pre-exposed values. If the cache scale is ece_cec​, a stored final-lighting texel is Lcardstored=ecL~cardL_{\rm card}^{\rm stored}=e_c\widetilde L_{\rm card}Lcardstored​=ec​Lcard​. Convert using the cache's scale when moving into scene-linear or view-pre-exposed space. The current view can have a different scale eve_vev​. A raw numeric comparison across these buffers is invalid until that conversion is explicit.

These paired views use the same source rectangle, x=200…999, y=0…679. Follow one stone cornice from the camera image into the coverage image: an accurate triangle hit can still land on a region without a usable cached shading value. Follow the broad cloth instead: coverage exists, but the cached representation has less spatial detail. Those are different errors, one of availability and one of resolution, and they need different fixes. Card coverage, scene inclusion, page residency, and texel resolution therefore require separate diagnosis. Magenta is the display color for a validity warning. The full diagnostic preserves the engine's original legend and frame.

Turn one card texel into a numerical lighting calculation

Choose a mapped texel on the narrow stone ledge along the left arcade. This is a declared query over captured card state, selected from the combine pass's tile list. This secondary surface lies approximately four metres above the floor at primary receiver A. Projecting its reconstructed card position into the hero view gives the marked point below.

Card 107 owns page 323. The page begins at physical atlas coordinate (2176,128) and spans 128 × 128 texels. Tile (13,1) begins at local coordinate (104,8), because a tile is 8 × 8. Taking thread coordinate (4,4) gives local texel (108,12), hence physical texel (2284,140). Sampling its center gives atlas UV ((2284+0.5)/4096,(140+0.5)/4096). Each addition changes the address; confusing a page-local coordinate with an atlas coordinate makes an otherwise valid lighting formula read another surface.

The stored albedo components are approximately (0.40000,0.37647,0.33725). Decode their square before using the material: effective linear albedo is (0.16000,0.14173,0.11374) for this capture's identity diffuse override. The direct irradiance atlas holds (4288,3296,2496), the indirect irradiance atlas holds (412,568,880), and emission is zero. All three lighting inputs use the cache's exposure scale. The combine therefore predicts, before the store:

The captured R11G11B10 output decodes to (240,174,122). The small change comes from storage: Unreal adds a coordinate/frame-seeded dither scaled by the target format's quantization step, then stores the unsigned floating-point channels. The replay's selected 8 × 8 tile matches all 64 captured output words under its stated store model. The model uses the test’s compressed-texture readback approximation. Agreement validates that approximation only at the samples compared here.

Cache exposure, bilinear taps, and the complete combine record

The cache uses CachedLightingPreExposure=1/16; the view uses PreExposure=1/2048. They are different scales. A stored final value of (240,174,122) becomes scene-linear (3840,2784,1952) after multiplying by 16, then view-pre-exposed (1.875,1.359375,0.953125) after multiplying by 1/2048. Multiplying the stored texel by the view scale alone loses a factor of 16. The same distinction applies when comparing direct card irradiance with primary-view SceneColor.

The complete query record retains the pass 694 parameter block, card orientation and bounds, page mapping, normalized depth 35404/65535, material/emissive/lighting inputs, four bilinear taps for every sampled atlas, cache/view exposure, frame seed, format quantization steps, and all 64 output comparisons. At this texel-center query the bilinear weights are (1,0,0,0); the neighboring tap values are still retained. At an off-center query all applicable weights would contribute.

The exporter decodes BC7/BC5 data to floating-point samples, discarding the original block encoding. The replay explicitly snaps those samples to a UNORM8 model before its material decode; the raw expanded values remain recorded. This is a modeling approximation. The arithmetic check validates this declared replay against the captured outputs, while native compressed-block equality remains outside its evidence. The source references and every payload hash are in the record.

Light the cards directly, then propagate card-to-card bounces

Direct card lighting evaluates the lights affecting the represented surface with its own shadowing path. In this snapshot, card lighting seeds mask tiles with attenuation, light-function and cloud-transmittance terms. It then traces distance fields or hardware rays for visibility. The primary view computes its VSM shadow result separately. It also cannot reuse the camera's final lit pixel: many card texels are off screen, and the receiver normal and material projection may differ. Light lists, shadow masks, card texel positions, and light parameters are therefore part of the cached computation.

For indirect lighting, distribute gather locations over card space, trace their directions, evaluate available scene radiance at hits, integrate irradiance, and reconstruct it across the card texels. These radiosity probes on cards update lighting on secondary surfaces. They are neither the camera's screen probes nor the separate world-space radiance-cache probes.

Place a radiosity probe by choosing a sample in the card's capture domain, decoding its surface depth, and transforming that point back into the scene. The gather follows the surface of the represented wall or column. Its normal and capture validity determine which surface is being sampled. A card-space grid drawn as a flat rectangle can hide this depth reconstruction; the scene view should place the samples on their reconstructed surfaces. The resulting low-order directional coefficients support a later irradiance reconstruction on that card. The camera pixel gets its diffuse output later, during reconstruction. Their four-coefficient, PDF-weighted hemisphere projection also has a different normalization from the screen probes' nine-coefficient sphere average.

Project the measured hemisphere with its units intact

A radiosity sample stores four coefficients per color channel: one constant basis function and three first-order directional functions. Let YjY_jYj​, j=0,…,3j=0,\ldots,3j=0,…,3, be that real SH basis, ece_cec​ the cache pre-exposure, and pHp_HpH​ the hemisphere sampling density. The source's coefficient estimator has the form

cjstored≈1N∑k=1NYj(ωk)ec L~i(ωk)pH(ωk),pH=12πfor the uniform-hemisphere permutation.c_j^{\rm stored}\approx\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N} Y_j(\omega_k)\frac{e_c\,\widetilde L_i(\omega_k)}{p_H(\omega_k)}, \qquad p_H=\frac{1}{2\pi}\quad\text{for the uniform-hemisphere permutation}.cjstored​≈N1​k=1∑N​Yj​(ωk​)pH​(ωk​)ec​Li​(ωk​)​,pH​=2π1​for the uniform-hemisphere permutation.

Y_j(\omega_k)\frac{e_c\,\widetilde L_i(\omega_k)}{p_H(\omega_k)},
\qquad p_H=\frac{1}{2\pi}\quad\text{for the uniform-hemisphere permutation}.

The PDF correction supplies the hemisphere measure. Use the radiosity normalization here. The screen probes’ extra factor belongs to their sphere-average representation. Irradiance is reconstructed by a dot product with the cosine-transfer coefficients: band zero receives π\piπ, and band one receives 2π/32\pi/32π/3. The resulting stored irradiance is divided by ece_cec​ to recover scene-referred irradiance; a unit-albedo Lambertian outgoing radiance divides once more by π\piπ. Here ec=0.0625e_c=0.0625ec​=0.0625, captured from the card-lighting parameter block.

The convention can be checked with a constant unit incident field over the surface hemisphere: its irradiance should be π\piπ, and its unit-albedo diffuse outgoing radiance should be 1. The independent 65,536-direction check reconstructs irradiance 3.14159811; the approximately 0.00017% residual against exact π\piπ comes from the source's rounded SH basis constants. That residual validates the normalization convention, but low-order SH still cannot reproduce every sharp lighting pattern: truncating the directional function remains an approximation.

Complete card and lighting records

The reference separates offline card construction, page allocation and address transforms, material capture, direct-light lists and shadows, and radiosity sampling and filtering. 10Share the incoming light field near the visible receiver

The Surface Cache made a secondary hit cheaper. We still cannot afford a large hemisphere of rays at every pixel. On the arcade floor, neighboring pixels on the same smooth patch see similar incident light. Trace a directional distribution at sparse surface positions, then reconstruct the lighting for neighboring pixels.

A screen probe is one such surface sample together with a directional representation of incoming radiance. “Screen” describes how Lumen chooses the sample. Its depth follows the sampled surface. Its origin comes from a surface position reconstructed using depth. The probe's normal, depth, material-related sampling information, and identity all have to be tracked.

Place probes before tracing rays

A minimal implementation chooses one depth sample per regular screen tile. That works for a flat floor and fails at silhouettes: a column may occupy only a few pixels and receive no representative. Add adaptive probes for uncovered depth/normal configurations. Budget and bound the adaptive count, assign stable indices, and write a map from pixels or tiles to candidate probe identities. Interpolation uses that map to find the probes assigned to each pixel. Allocation order alone gives no pixel ownership information.

Invalid depth, sky pixels, backface-supported materials, thin geometry, and normal discontinuities need explicit handling. A probe origin displaced too far from the surface can cross a wall. Too little offset can self-intersect. Jitter changes the sample pattern over time and must be recorded alongside temporal reprojection. Quality settings determine the probe spacing and directional resolution.

Slide the camera sideways while keeping one screen tile highlighted. Its depth sample can move along the floor, cross a column silhouette, and then land on the far wall. The tile index has stayed the same while the represented surface has changed. A temporal probe display has to show world positions or geometric correspondence as well as atlas indices. Reusing coefficients solely because the integer index matches would carry one surface's illumination onto another. The adaptive count and compacted order follow current demand. The same index can refer to different world locations on successive updates.

Build the first working placement and gather pipeline

Use separate records for the receiver and the traced directions. A minimal receiver record contains world position, geometric/shading normal as required, device or linear depth with a declared convention, screen coordinate, and validity. A ray record contains its owning probe, directional cell, refinement level, direction, trace interval, and result state. Compaction changes queue order, so an atlas coordinate cannot stand in for the owner identity.

// Teaching implementation: five dispatches with explicit dependencies.
PlaceUniform:
    for each screen tile:
        choose a valid depth sample using the frame's declared jitter
        reconstruct world position with this view's inverse projection
        write UniformProbe[tile] and its geometry

FindUnrepresented:
    for each valid pixel:
        test the uniform probe against this pixel's depth and normal
        if incompatible: mark a demand in an adaptive allocation cell

AllocateAdaptive:
    prefix-sum unique demands; cap at the allocated capacity
    write AdaptiveProbe[base + offset] and pixel/cell-to-probe indirection
    record overflow explicitly; never write beyond the probe array

GenerateDirections:
    for each valid uniform or adaptive probe:
        generate the directional cell/refinement records
        write owner indices before any later queue compaction

TraceAndReconstruct:
    trace the screen route; compact unresolved records
    trace the selected world route; fill each original result slot
    reconstruct directional cells; integrate and interpolate to pixels

A prefix sum is a parallel version of assigning consecutive indices to marked items. If demand flags are [1,0,1,1], an exclusive prefix sum is [0,1,1,2]; the marked items write to indices 0,1,2 and the total count is 3. For several demands in the same allocation cell, deduplicate or use one atomic claim before scanning. Otherwise repeated pixels spend the entire adaptive budget on the same surface.

On the GPU, put the count and capacity in different fields. The count determines active work; capacity determines legal addresses. A subsequent indirect dispatch uses the compacted count, rounded up to the thread-group size, while every shader guards its final partial group. The render graph must order producer writes before consumers and declare the access transition. A CPU readback of the count between every stage would serialize the frame and erase much of the benefit.

The captured Sponza frame shows what happens when stored entries and active entries are confused. Its placement allocation has 3,600 uniform slots and capacity for 1,800 adaptive probes. The captured adaptive allocator says 117, supported by 117 nonzero entries in the tile header. Of the uniform slots, 3,569 have finite positive geometry, giving 3,686 active placements with usable geometry. Scanning the entire storage for positive values would instead find 3,809: 123 additional adaptive entries contain old values beyond the active allocation. Drawing those stale entries as current probes would make the visualization wrong even though every plotted coordinate was read from a real buffer. The placement record retains both the active subset and the excluded storage, with the allocator/header evidence and its readback limitations.

Production adds classification, allocation, and packed representations, but every returned direction must still stay associated with the receiver and directional measure that generated it. A probe visualization needs the placement map, adaptive count, ray index mapping, and validity data alongside the radiance atlas.

Storing incoming radiance by direction

Suppose the courtyard is bright to the right and the covered arcade is dark to the left. Two surfaces at the same position but with different normals receive different irradiance. A single average color loses that difference. Store radiance as a function of direction, then integrate it against the receiving material.

The inspected implementation uses equal-area spherical mapping for the directional probes that need it. Ordinary two-channel octahedral normal encoding assigns unequal solid angles. Substituting it would change the integration weights. The mapping function, resolution, bin centers, randomized offsets, and Jacobian determine how a texel corresponds to a direction and measure. A visualization should show that mapping beside the radiance, because a bright atlas texel is meaningless without its represented direction.

In the simplest implementation, trace one jittered direction in each equal-area bin. For M bins covering the sphere, each bin has solid angle 4π/M4\pi/M4π/M. Sum radiance times the positive receiver cosine and this measure to estimate irradiance. If directions instead come from a probability distribution, use their inverse-PDF weights. A quadrature weight gives an area to integrate. A stochastic PDF describes the likelihood of drawing a sample there.

Spend directions where the material and illumination need them

A diffuse receiver prefers directions with a large cosine; a glossy receiver prefers directions near its reflection lobe. The last frame's lighting also predicts where bright incoming directions may lie. Lumen's probe tracing can use BRDF and lighting information to guide its directional work. This requires both a distribution and a reproducible mapping from sample indices to generated directions.

To implement a first importance sampler, build nonnegative bin weights aja_jaj​, add a small support floor, normalize to Pj=aj/∑kakP_j=a_j/\sum_k a_kPj​=aj​/∑k​ak​, select a bin through a cumulative distribution or hierarchical reduction, then sample within it. If its solid angle is Δσj\Delta\sigma_jΔσj​ and sampling within the bin is uniform, the directional PDF is pσ=Pj/Δσjp_\sigma=P_j/\Delta\sigma_jpσ​=Pj​/Δσj​. The generated sample must retain enough information to reconstruct that PDF or its encoded reciprocal weight.

At a shared probe, multiple nearby materials may request different distributions. Building the guide from represented BRDF information is an approximation to their combined demand. Quantization, limited directional bins, support floors, maximum ray weights, and radiance clamps can change the estimator. Assess bias across the whole probe pipeline, including reconstruction and reuse.

The Lumen implementation uses a structured refinement scheme. Its normalized incoming-light PDF and BRDF PDF form a sort key. Low-priority ray slots can be reassigned in groups of three to subdivide a higher-priority spherical cell into four children. The default production path uses one refinement level; the serial reference path supports multiple levels. The packed ray information retains that cell and refinement level. The traced results are subsequently reconstructed into the regular directional representation before filtering and integration. Use the PDF to rank cells. Dividing the reconstructed radiance by it a second time would change the result. See ray ranking and subdivision and integration of the reconstructed directional field.

Trace the generated directions through the screen/world hierarchy. An accepted screen hit uses its valid screen-lighting source. A world hit queries the represented surface lighting or selected hit-lighting path. A miss may query the sky. Store the result, hit distance or depth, validity, and any additional flags needed by later filtering. Record whether the stored value is raw radiance, weighted radiance, or a packed trace result. The integration formula must match that storage contract.

The counts describe probe allocation in this diagnostic frame. Hit validity requires trace results, and a later diagnostic frame can allocate a different adaptive set.

Every available field for the three selected probes

The records for probe A, probe B, and probe C retain all 64 trace slots each: packed ray-info words, cell/level, jitter samples, reconstructed directions and cone widths, trace radiance, stored hit words and flags, recorded hit distances where valid, projected hit checks, and the separately addressed regular radiance values.
