Read one probe at a time. Select a probe on the arcade floor and locate the atlas block assigned to it. Identify the bins looking into the courtyard and those looking at the nearby wall. Compare their radiance and hit-distance values, then inspect the trace or fallback that supplied each. Finally rotate the receiving normal in the integration diagram. The same directional data should produce a different cosine-weighted result without requiring a different stored incoming field.

Long traces still repeat work. Many nearby probes look through the same opening toward distant geometry or sky, so one more cache in world space can share that work. Its purpose differs from the Surface Cache's.

11Cache distant incoming light in world space

A world-space radiance probe stores a directional incoming field at a point in space. It answers a different question from a card texel: the card stores a surface's approximate outgoing radiance, while the world probe describes what arrives from each direction at a spatial location. Screen probes sample the visible receivers. World probes can share far-field information between those receivers and across camera movement.

Allocate where queries actually need the field

A dense fine grid over the entire world is too expensive. Clipmaps provide a fine region near the view and progressively coarser coverage farther away. Demand marks identify cells needed by current gathers. An indirection texture or buffer maps those cells to physical probe indices. Allocation tracks free entries, last use, update priority, and validity. Scrolling a clipmap changes the relationship between logical cells and world positions, so stale entries cannot remain valid under their old coordinates.

Screen-probe placement and cache demand therefore precede the relevant cache update. The implementation schedule is a dependency graph: place receivers, mark demanded world cells, allocate or update the selected world probes, then consume the available cache in the remaining traces. Other consumers and retained data can have their own update paths.

For each selected world probe, trace a directional distribution and store radiance plus geometric information needed for parallax and visibility handling. Construct the configured filtered representation and borders so directional lookups remain coherent across seams. The inspected default stores one radiance-cache mip. Additional mips are configurable. An atlas slot with radiance but no valid depth or position record is insufficient for a reliable spatial reconstruction.

Move the camera a short distance. A world probe can remain at the same world location even though its projected position changes. For a larger move, a clipmap scroll brings new cells into range; a physical atlas slot may eventually be reassigned to one of them. Track the world cell and allocation identity together. For a fixed-camera light change, try the opposite experiment: keep the spatial grid fixed while the stored directional radiance changes. Placement, allocation, selection for update, and stored illumination are four distinct observations. A placement overlay alone measures only the first of them.

All grid positions, hidden probes, and temporal correspondence

The motion ledger records unchanged cells, changed logical coordinates, recycled physical slots, additions, removals, last-use and last-trace timestamps. The baseline record retains every active probe's address and position, plus allocator/free-list checks. Its 925 allocated high-water slots minus 47 free slots equal the 878 active references. The separate hidden-probe projection reveals cells behind primary geometry without mixing them into the visible marker plot.

These are the screen-probe gather's main radiance-cache cells: four 48³ clipmaps, identified through matching mark/allocate parameters and resource-consumer bindings. The separate translucency cache uses three 24³ clipmaps in this capture. Combining a transform from one renderer invocation with resources from another, or selecting the translucency cache by a similar resource name, produces a plausible but incorrect visualization. The source records identify the selected invocation and every consumed version. Position markers locate the main cache’s probes. Their directional data live in its octahedral atlas. The screen probes use a separate SH layout.

Implement a small world-probe allocator before adding clipmaps

Start with one bounded 3D grid and a physical pool of P probe slots. Store an indirection index per grid cell, initialized to an invalid sentinel. Store world position, allocation generation, last-used update, last-lit update, and validity per physical slot. The directional radiance and depth atlases use that physical index. The generation prevents a delayed request from mistaking a recycled slot for its previous owner.

A demand pass marks cells touched by queries. A compacted demand list allocates missing slots from a free list. A separate update list selects at most B probes according to a deterministic priority. Clear or initialize every newly assigned slot before any interpolation can consume it. After tracing and filtering, publish its valid state. Retire unused slots only after their current readers have finished; freeing a slot early can recycle storage that the GPU is still reading.

For cell size h and grid origin o, a position x has grid coordinate q = (x−o)/h. The integer part identifies neighboring cells; the fractional part supplies interpolation coordinates. A corner with bits (bₓ,bᵧ,b_z) has spatial weight equal to the product of fᵢ for bit 1 and (1−fᵢ) for bit 0. All eight weights sum to one. Missing corners and geometric rejection change that sum, so track the accepted weight explicitly. The elementary implementation tests addressing and constants. Near Sponza’s walls, interpolation also needs to respect visibility.

Add camera-centred clipmaps only after the single grid works. When a grid scrolls, distinguish cells that retain the same world location from new entering cells. Wrapped storage indices alone cannot establish that identity. Allocate, invalidate, and update against world cell coordinates or an equivalent tagged mapping. The engine's indirection layout and budgeting policy handle the same ownership problem in more detail.

Why ordinary trilinear interpolation leaks through walls

Take two probes on opposite sides of an arcade wall. Their positions are close, but their incoming fields are different. A distance-only interpolation gives the dark side some of the bright side's field. Weights that sum to one reproduce a constant field exactly. Across a wall they can still blend unrelated lighting.

A teaching reconstruction starts with L~i(x,ω)=∑mwm(x,ω)L^i(xm,ωm)\widetilde L_i(x,\omega)=\sum_m w_m(x,\omega)\widehat L_i(x_m,\omega_m)Li​(x,ω)=∑m​wm​(x,ω)Li​(xm​,ωm​), with normalized valid weights. The direction ωm\omega_mωm​ may be corrected for the difference between the query point and the probe's observed hit. A depth estimate helps decide whether that correction is plausible and whether the query lies in front of or behind a represented occluder. The engine implementation adds specific clipmap selection, coverage tests, fade distances, interpolation weights, and directional/depth sampling rules; a generic eight-probe average loses those conditions.

Local geometry must still be resolved before relying on a distant cache answer. A near wall should occlude far radiance. The trace/cache transition distance and cone footprint determine when a cache approximation is useful. Querying the cache from the origin without local visibility would illuminate the arcade through its own wall.

coverage = choose_cache_clipmap_and_coverage(query_position, ray_cone)
if not coverage.valid: continue_world_trace_or_return_explicit_failure
neighbors = read_probe_indirection(coverage.cell_corners)
for probe in valid(neighbors):
    geometry = read_probe_position_and_directional_depth(probe)
    direction = parallax_correct(query_position, ray_direction, geometry)
    weight = spatial_weight * validity_and_visibility_weight
    value += weight * sample_probe_radiance(probe, direction, mip)
    total_weight += weight
if total_weight == 0: use_documented_fallback
else: value /= total_weight

The pseudocode lists the decisions needed for reconstruction. Consult the shader for the exact order of operations. A failed coverage lookup, an unallocated indirection entry, a valid zero-radiance probe, and a rejected geometric contribution are four distinct states. Log them separately. Otherwise a black output cannot tell you which part of the cache failed.

Evaluate one actual eight-probe neighborhood

The captured world-cache pass contains 104,483 compacted trace entries. Select lane 11 by the declared selection rule in the query record. Its packed word identifies uniform screen probe 695 and trace cell (1,4), stored at trace-buffer coordinate (441,68). The probe lies near screen (882,136). Its reconstructed translated-world query position is (499.349,144.104,251.590) cm, and its sampled world direction is approximately (0.916132,−0.394151,0.073122).

This query falls inside clipmap 0, whose cell size is 104.1667 cm. Subtract its translated-world corner, divide by cell size, and subtract the half-cell offset used for probe centers. The base interpolation cell is (29,25,27), with fractions (0.633747,0.383396,0.279266). Read the eight integer entries of the 192 × 48 × 48 indirection volume; they map these logical neighbors to physical probe indices 38,715,42,719,39,716,45,720. A screen probe index, a clipmap cell coordinate, and a physical world-probe index are three different address spaces.

The trilinear weights, in the record's neighbor order, are approximately (0.162765,0.063068,0.101205,0.039215,0.281642,0.109129,0.175121,0.067855); they sum to 1. Spatial weighting alone is insufficient. Each probe uses its captured position and directional depth to reproject the query direction onto the probe's assumed bounding sphere. That changes the directional atlas coordinates and introduces the solid-angle correction. Read all four bilinear taps at those coordinates, decode their R11G11B10 values, undo the cached exposure by multiplying by 16, and apply the recorded parallax factor before the spatial interpolation.

12From directional probe samples to surface lighting

The renderer has sparse, noisy samples taken at different surfaces, in different directions and at different times. At each visible receiver it must reconstruct the incoming light field and integrate it against that surface's scattering response. A measurement from an earlier frame can help only while it still describes the same surface under the same illumination.

Integrate the directional field

A diffuse surface needs irradiance E(n)=∫Li(ω)max⁡(0,n⋅ω)dσE(n)=\int L_i(\omega)\max(0,n\cdot\omega)d\sigmaE(n)=∫Li​(ω)max(0,n⋅ω)dσ. This is a convolution with a broad cosine kernel, so it discards much of the high-frequency directional detail that a mirror needs. Its width makes low-order directional bases useful for diffuse lighting.

Spherical harmonics (SH) are an orthonormal basis of functions on the sphere, analogous to Fourier modes on a circle. A coefficient is an integral of the function times one basis function. The constant basis term carries the mean; higher bands record increasingly fine directional variation. Three bands contain nine coefficients. Cosine convolution multiplies the first three bands by A0=πA_0=\piA0​=π, A1=2π/3A_1=2\pi/3A1​=2π/3, and A2=π/4A_2=\pi/4A2​=π/4. Truncating there is an approximation, particularly for sharp occlusion and narrow light sources.

Normalization must match the stored representation. In the inspected screen-probe filtering path, the stored radiance SH is formed as an average over the equal-area sphere samples:

slm≈1M∑j=1MLjYlm(ωj),E(n)≈4π∑l=02∑m=−llAlslmYlm(n).s_{lm}\approx\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^{M}L_jY_{lm}(\omega_j),\qquad E(n)\approx4\pi\sum_{l=0}^{2}\sum_{m=-l}^{l}A_l s_{lm}Y_{lm}(n).slm​≈M1​j=1∑M​Lj​Ylm​(ωj​),E(n)≈4πl=0∑2​m=−l∑l​Al​slm​Ylm​(n).
LaTeX source
s_{lm}\approx\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^{M}L_jY_{lm}(\omega_j),\qquad
E(n)\approx4\pi\sum_{l=0}^{2}\sum_{m=-l}^{l}A_l s_{lm}Y_{lm}(n).

The factor 4π converts a sphere average into an integral. It must appear exactly once. The default irradiance storage path preintegrates the result into a 6×6 equal-area directional probe with a border (the engine names this format OCT); the SH3 storage path retains the coefficients and applies the factor at consumption. SH3 can be selected explicitly and is also forced when the configured short-range bent-normal AO path applies during integration. The card-radiosity SH path uses a different, PDF-weighted hemisphere projection with four coefficients. Derive the scale from this representation’s own measure.

A normalization test. For constant radiance L₀, only the constant SH coefficient is nonzero in the exact projection. Since Y00=1/4πY_{00}=1/\sqrt{4\pi}Y00​=1/4π​, the stored average coefficient is s00=L0/4πs_{00}=L_0/\sqrt{4\pi}s00​=L0​/4π​. Substitution gives E=4π π L0/(4π)=πL0E=4\pi\,\pi\,L_0/(4\pi)=\pi L_0E=4ππL0​/(4π)=πL0​, exactly the hemisphere integral. Omitting 4π gives L₀/4 instead. A scale error of this kind persists at any sample count.

At a captured probe position, evaluate the reconstructed unit-albedo diffuse response for many hypothetical receiver normals. Draw each normal as a direction from the probe and use the response magnitude as the distance along it. The resulting lobe is a graph of a function, placed in the scene where that function was measured. A long upward lobe means a surface with an upward normal would receive more reconstructed diffuse illumination there. Its orientation can be compared with Sponza's opening; its value at the actual receiver normal can be compared with the integrated buffer.

For a temporal comparison, retain the same units, angular basis, exposure conversion, radius scale, and color mapping. Rescaling each lobe to its own maximum would make a fourfold drop in illumination disappear from the picture. Low-order reconstruction can also produce negative lobes near sharp changes. If the display clips negative values to zero, report the clipping and retain the signed coefficients for reconstruction. A changing lobe at a fixed position describes a changing estimated field. A lobe that jumps to another surface after camera motion instead needs a new geometric correspondence before its coefficients can be compared.

Focused positions, signed coefficients, and temporal matches

The lobes use captured coefficients and the captured camera transform; their meshes and colors are a CPU visualization of the reconstructed function. They evaluate the no-occlusion, unit-albedo response. They show the directional function before receiver materials or base color enter the calculation. Use the placement view to locate a sample, then use its lobe to ask which receiver orientations would receive the strongest reconstructed illumination there.

The light-step example also shows why temporal matching needs geometry. The focused left-arcade sample labelled arcade-left-8 has nearest matches within 5.35 cm and normal dot products above 0.999 across these five observations. Several floor matches move roughly half a metre because a small screen-space jitter produces a large world-space displacement at a grazing view angle; the data flags these as incompatible under its stated matching rule. A lobe can jump when its sample moves to another surface. Check the world position before attributing the jump to a lighting change. To match samples across frames, the records retain their positions, normals, matching distances and all 27 signed coefficient values.

Separate normalization error from quadrature error. The decoder evaluates the constant-field test above with the analytic constant coefficient and obtains D=1 within 1.5×10−6 over 256 test normals. Projecting that same synthetic constant field through the actual 8×8 direction layout leaves small higher-band residuals; the worst deviation becomes about 2.05%. The first test checks the factor 4π and the Lambert factor. The second exposes the finite directional quadrature. Both tests feed the decoder a synthetic constant field with a known answer.

The screen-probe diffuse output is the unit-albedo diffuse response, D=E/πD=E/\piD=E/π, multiplied by the view pre-exposure. Composition later multiplies D by the visible receiver's diffuse color. The receiver albedo and 1/π must each be applied exactly once. By contrast, the Surface Cache's final-lighting combine has already multiplied secondary direct-plus-indirect irradiance by the secondary surface's effective albedo/π and added emission. Its separate direct and indirect irradiance atlases remain unweighted by that albedo. Those two material interactions belong to different path vertices.

Interpolate only between compatible surfaces

Choose nearby probe candidates through the screen/adaptive-probe maps. Compute geometric weights using position, depth, and normal compatibility. Normalize accepted weights. If every candidate fails, take an explicit fallback. Dividing by a tiny remaining weight can amplify noise. At a silhouette, adjacent pixels can land metres apart in world space and receive very different lighting.

Spatial filtering of probe radiance also needs geometric checks. A ray hit distance helps distinguish an observed nearby wall from distant illumination. Position and angular thresholds limit mixing between incompatible observations. Several small filter passes can be cheaper than one large kernel, but their combined footprint still smooths the field. Inspect contacts and thin columns as well as the flat floor.

History records a previous measurement

For a moving camera, the previous value at the same screen coordinate usually belongs to another world point. Reproject the current receiver into the previous frame using transforms and motion. Gather neighboring history taps, then validate each tap against depth, normal, material classification, and availability. Exclude invalid taps and renormalize. Occlusion changes create disocclusions: a newly visible surface has no valid previous observation, even when a nearby color looks plausible.

For valid history, a simplified blend is Ht=(1−at)Ht−1reprojected+atCtH_t=(1-a_t)H_{t-1}^{\rm reprojected}+a_t C_tHt​=(1−at​)Ht−1reprojected​+at​Ct​. A running-average weight at=1/(N+1)a_t=1/(N+1)at​=1/(N+1) reduces the influence of each new noisy estimate as N grows. Capping N bounds the latency. Fast-update flags, neighborhood clamps, invalid-current-sample handling, and rejection can alter this rule in the actual shader. The final per-pixel temporal accumulation follows integration; there are also separate histories used earlier for probe radiance and sampling guidance. Each history belongs to the stage that reads and updates it.

If history stores view-pre-exposed lighting, it also needs the ratio of current and previous pre-exposure. Reprojection can identify the correct point yet still produce a brightness jump if the exposure conversion is missing. Camera cuts, resolution changes, incompatible view rectangles, and changes to the representation require history invalidation or a defined resampling path.

The latency tradeoff in numbers. After a step from old value 0 to a constant new value 1, an exponential blend with a=0.1 gives 0.1, 0.19, 0.271, and after ten updates about 0.651. Stable accumulation intentionally remembers the old value. A still screenshot cannot reveal that delay. A camera-motion sequence and a light-change sequence test different causes of history failure.

Short-range occlusion supplies local geometric detail that sparse probes can miss. Ambient occlusion or a bent normal can modify the diffuse and specular reconstruction, but these are additional approximations with explicit ownership. Multiplying every lighting term by an arbitrary AO value can darken direct illumination twice. Match the selected shader path's AO application and show its buffer with the receiver geometry when diagnosing a contact.

Increase the new-sample weight to respond faster. For independent stationary input noise, the steady-state variance ratio is a/(2−a), obtained by solving v = (1−a)²v + a²σ². That assumption excludes correlated samples and changing illumination. The curve models a valid exponential history; Unreal's rejection and fast-update logic deliberately depart from it.

History masks, SH layouts, and exact normalization

The filtering reference and temporal reference retain the shader data contracts. The main source operations are sphere-average SH and irradiance generation, unit-albedo diffuse output, and per-tap validity and accumulation. These links identify the selected implementation, while the equations above explain why its scale and validity metadata are needed.

13Sampling, tracing and reconstructing glossy reflections

Return to C, the polished test sphere. A diffuse probe can tolerate a broad angular reconstruction because the receiver integrates over a hemisphere. The polished sphere asks a much narrower question: what lies near the reflected direction? Low-order SH cannot retain the detailed image of Sponza's columns and balconies, so reflections need a dedicated route.

Classify the receivers before allocating ray work

Read roughness and shading-model data from the primary GBuffer. Classify tiles that require dedicated reflection work, allocate ray records, and generate reflected or microfacet-sampled directions with the information needed to interpret their sampling density. Trace the screen representation first when enabled, then compact unresolved rays into the selected world tracing path. Store hit information and radiance in buffers whose indices map back to the originating pixel or downsampled sample.

Begin with an explicit receiver-to-ray mapping. A tile containing a polished sphere and a rough stone wall may need dedicated rays for only some pixels. The classification mask says which receivers participate; the compacted work list says which records will be dispatched. A downsampled trace grid also needs its selected full-resolution sample offset. Without those mappings, a correct traced radiance can be reconstructed onto the wrong side of the sphere. Clear rejected entries to a declared invalid state before sparse writes, and pass the active count to subsequent indirect dispatches.

In the inspected tile classification shader, NeedRayTracedReflections sets the reflection bit after the material's smooth-bias adjustment. The later list builder turns these flags into indirect work lists. A set bit requests work. Trace results and lighting values appear in later resources.

Sampling the glossy integral

Let Li,RL_{i,R}Li,R​ denote the incident field assigned to the scene-reflection branch after the direct-light ownership split. The target at a receiver is

L_{i,R}(x,\omega_i)\,\max(0,n\cdot\omega_i)\,d\sigma(\omega_i).

A perfect mirror selects one direction, but a rough reflector has a distribution of contributing directions. Rays near the mirror direction can hit different columns, see different lights or escape to the sky. Blurring one mirror sample afterward loses those differences. Use the visible-normal microfacet sampler derived earlier to generate plausible half-vectors, reflect the outgoing direction, and convert the half-vector PDF into a directional PDF. Keep geometric-sidedness rejection and the perfect-specular limit explicit.

This is the estimator a minimal reference implementation should make correct. The production renderer distributes factors across ray generation, trace payloads, resolve and final BRDF combination. To recover the final R, account for the factors still missing at each intermediate texture. It can also bias direction selection, limit ray intensity, downsample, and reuse nearby samples to control cost and variance. Each such choice needs a matching weight or an explicit approximation. A narrower sampling distribution without the corresponding PDF correction changes the brightness as well as the noise.

// Minimal reference contract; production buffer packing and weighting differ.
receiver = decode_primary_interaction(pixel)
(wi, pdf) = sample_specular_direction(receiver, random_sample)
if pdf <= 0 or unsupported_geometric_side(receiver, wi): return invalid
ray = {origin, wi, pixel, pdf, roughness, validity}
hit = trace_scene_representations(ray)
Li = evaluate_owned_incident_field(hit, ray)
sample = specular_bsdf(receiver, wi) * Li * positive_cosine / pdf
store(sample, hit.distance, receiver_geometry, validity)

At the production storage boundary, Ray generation writes a direction, a signed cone/inverse-PDF field, and a trace distance. The rough branch uses visible-GGX sampling; its inverse-PDF field is clamped, and its sign also carries the first-person flag. Trace throughput is initialized separately to one. Ray generation stores the direction and inverse-PDF data here. The reference pseudocode combines those quantities with the BSDF in one step. The ordinary sampler also biases one random coordinate by 1 − GGXSamplingBias (default 0.9), without a separate correction for that truncation. The production path accepts bias to reduce variance relative to the reference microfacet estimator.

Carry unresolved rays across representations

The screen trace and world trace answer the same ray query with different geometric information. Preserve the ray's origin, direction, remaining interval, owner, and accepted-hit state when compacting unresolved work. An uncertain HZB crossing needs another visibility test. A ray that leaves the screen can still hit offscreen geometry. Only the selected continuation route can establish what the available world representation contains along that direction. The tracing chapter supplies the common intersection contract; reflection payloads additionally retain the information needed for hit shading and glossy reconstruction.

A hit distance serves two jobs. It identifies the secondary intersection for shading, and it helps the reconstruction reason about parallax and footprint. A nearby reflected lamp and the distant sky can have similar colors while requiring very different history correspondences. Give misses an explicit validity flag and environment policy so a distant hit remains distinguishable. Preserve those states through resolve even when both routes eventually produce RGB.

There is also a second kind of compaction: the compaction modes select misses for continuation, or select hits whose material record requests another lighting pass. To interpret a compacted entry, read the queue’s selection predicate and payload. Some queues also carry hits. Screen tracing also consumes a previous SceneColor sample, so its returned color already carries a temporal and shading approximation in addition to screen-space geometry limitations.

Resolve sparse samples without dragging reflections through time

Resolve these sparse samples into a specular signal using geometry, roughness, hit distance, and temporal information. A glossy reflection can have a very different apparent motion from its primary surface; blindly reusing the surface's diffuse history rule can drag a reflection across the object. Distance and roughness inform reconstruction footprints, while disocclusions and mismatched hits must reduce reuse.

Consider a smooth mirror fixed to the wall while the camera moves sideways. The wall point has one geometric motion correspondence, but the image of a column inside the mirror shifts according to the reflected view. Reprojecting only the wall can therefore find a previous pixel with the wrong reflected column. At a rough surface the response covers a wider angular neighborhood, so reconstruction can tolerate a broader footprint; at a sharp surface that same reuse erases detail. Geometry validation and roughness-dependent weighting determine which radiance samples enter the estimate.

Build reconstruction in stages. First display independent current samples with validity and hit distance. Then resolve to the output grid using known receiver mappings and compatibility weights. Add history reprojection and explicit rejection, keeping the current estimate available as a fallback. Finally add the selected variance reduction and neighborhood constraints. For each stage, retain whether the signal is raw incident radiance, a partially weighted estimate, or an already reconstructed specular contribution, and convert previous/current pre-exposure consistently. Applying base color or Fresnel again at composition would weight the reflection twice.

In the production resolve, the sample weight is the microfacet distribution value divided by the stored ray PDF. It applies weights to accepted center and neighbor samples, then divides accumulated lighting by accumulated weight. This reconstruction normalizes partially weighted radiance. The per-path estimator above applies the full BSDF weight. It still needs the receiver's environment-BRDF factor at composition. The ordinary opaque composition branch blends rough and traced signals and then multiplies by EnvBRDF; clear coat takes a separate layered branch.

Conditional compilation decides which rejection tests run. In this version, the proposed normal/roughness lobe-confidence test is disabled by LOBE_CONFIDENCE=0 in the temporal shader. The hit-history plane-depth test is also disabled. Active logic instead uses validity and depth/distance checks, neighborhood clamping, and a choice between surface and reflected-hit histories based on neighborhood error. Roughness still controls accumulation limits, and the separate spatial filter uses a roughness-dependent radius and normal acceptance cone. Attribute the rejection here to the spatial filter. The temporal lobe test was inactive.

Separate the ray hit from its lighting

At a secondary hit, Surface Cache mode returns a cheap effective diffuse response. Hit-lighting modes evaluate selected material and lighting terms at the actual hit. They can recover directional specular effects that a direction-independent card cannot represent. However, hit lighting is still a real-time estimator with finite tracing, selected source evaluation, and continued cache reuse for some indirect terms.

Consider a polished sphere reflecting another metallic object. Correct triangle visibility only identifies the second object. If its lighting comes from a fully rough card response, its reflected appearance can still differ from the path tracer. Tracing and secondary shading therefore need separate treatment in both code and comparisons.

The hardware trace's completion logic decides whether a hit still requires hit lighting. Successful scene-color reuse can complete a hit; valid radiance-cache coverage can complete a continuation. Sky is added on a remaining miss when enabled, while the optional skylight-leaking term is a separate artistic approximation that can also affect hits. Intensity clamping controls fireflies. None of those operations establishes a fully recursive reference solution. The capture at C used Surface Cache lighting. Material hit lighting follows a separate route.

The material-detail camera makes the angular question visible without changing the hero view used for the atrium's other diagnostics. The three metal spheres share linear base color (1, 0.766, 0.336) and metallic value 1; the three gray spheres share base color (0.8, 0.8, 0.8) and metallic value 0. Their different roughness values change the scattering integral. The surrounding stone and cloth provide recognizable structures in that integral.

Inspect the reflected signal independently of the material

At C, the captured resolved specular signal is (0.0180664,0.0135498,0.0087891), while the later specular-indirect output is (0.0166016,0.0144043,0.0085449), both view-pre-exposed. The resolved hit depth is 273.75 cm. These values and their distinct versions are retained in the reflection record. The changes between these stages come from reconstruction and history processing. Base color enters through its own material term.

Even the history counter needs its own decode contract. This reflection path stores count/32 in a UNORM target. C’s raw byte 96 decodes to (96/255) × 32 ≈ 12.047 effective accumulated frames. Spatial and temporal interpolation can make that value nonintegral. The screen-probe history uses a different packed format, with four bits for fast-update amount and four for a normalized count. Check the encoding of each resource before decoding it.

Blending overlapping specular estimates

For sufficiently rough surfaces, the screen-probe path supplies a rough specular approximation. The dedicated traced-reflection path covers lower roughness. Where their ranges overlap, they estimate overlapping illumination and need a blend. In the ordinary opaque Lumen branch,

αr=saturate⁡(rmax⁡−rΔr),R=(1−αr)Rrough+αrRtraced.\alpha_r=\operatorname{saturate}\left(\frac{r_{\max}-r}{\Delta r}\right),\qquad R=(1-\alpha_r)R_{\rm rough}+\alpha_rR_{\rm traced}.αr​=saturate(Δrrmax​−r​),R=(1−αr​)Rrough​+αr​Rtraced​.

R=(1-\alpha_r)R_{\rm rough}+\alpha_rR_{\rm traced}.

The inspected default post-process threshold is 0.4 with a default fade length of 0.1; the capture manifest records the actual overrides. At roughness 0.2 the ordinary formula gives fully traced weight; at 0.35 it gives half; at 0.5 it gives none. These are workload and reconstruction decisions. A material can still reflect light on either side of the 0.4 roughness threshold. Clear coat, backface-diffuse materials, SSR, water, and translucent front layers have other branches.

With the sphere roughness held fixed, changing the tracing cutoff selects how the renderer estimates the same physical reflection. Changing material roughness with the cutoff fixed alters the target integral. Keeping these tests separate prevents a quality-setting effect from being explained as a material law.

The analytic direct-light pass already evaluates the material's specular response to its owned lights. Exclude direct connections already evaluated elsewhere when composing the dedicated scene reflection. The final composition follows the source partition, lobe partition, and representation blend together.

Reflection state and mode-specific implementation

The reflection reference documents tile classification, downsample factors, trace hit/throughput/background state, fallback, resolve, and history. The ordinary blend factor is defined in LumenReflectionsCombine.ush. The composition reference explains which signals are already BRDF weighted and which still need the receiver material.

14Assemble one frame and account for every contribution

The renderer now contains several RGB images with very different meanings. Some hold primary material data, some incoming radiance, some irradiance, and some an already multiplied material response. Some use cache pre-exposure and others view pre-exposure. A unit or ownership mistake here shifts the whole image systematically.

For the simplified opaque Default Lit configuration, the remaining diffuse response is Dstored=evER/πD^{\rm stored}=e_vE_R/\piDstored=ev​ER​/π. Multiply it by the receiver diffuse color. The reflected scene specular signal is chosen or blended according to its route, then receives the corresponding specular response through the composition stage's environment-BRDF factor. Add these to the correctly owned emissive and analytic-direct contributions in the same view-pre-exposed space. The precise production composite also contains occlusion, layered-material, reflection-scaling, and platform branches documented in the reference.

The GBuffer supplies material inputs such as albedo. The Surface Cache stores indirect irradiance on represented surfaces. Screen probes reconstruct a diffuse response for the pixel, and a world probe stores directional radiance that still needs integration to yield irradiance. These distinctions explain why the buffer views identify units, encoding, exposure, coordinate mapping, producer, and validity alongside their displayed colors.

The dependency graph an implementation must schedule

Build scene representations and capture dirty card material pages. Build or update tracing acceleration structures and distance fields. Update selected card direct lighting and radiosity with their intervening final-lighting combines. Rasterize the primary depth/material state and construct the screen hierarchies and visible-light shadow data. Place screen probes and build their guides. Mark and update demanded world-cache probes, trace and filter incoming lighting, integrate at receivers, and apply valid history. Trace and reconstruct the selected reflection work. Compose the owned lighting contributions and run the display pipeline.

Some of these tasks can overlap. Unreal's render graph handles resource dependencies, and the renderer separates asynchronous gather work from later composition to overlap eligible work with direct lighting. C++ records pass order. Measure GPU execution time with GPU timestamps. To profile the system, inspect dispatch dimensions, active lists, resource sizes, queue dependencies, and actual GPU timestamps. Sum mutually exclusive GPU intervals. Use comparable instrumentation for both frames so capture overhead stays out of the algorithm comparison.

A practical implementation ladder

Build a correct subset before adding reuse. Begin with rasterized primary surfaces plus exact direct shadow rays and a reference path tracer. Add a single diffuse surface cache with known coordinates; compare its hit response against the reference at the same point. Add virtual pages only after the nonvirtual lookup is correct. Add sparse screen probes on a flat surface, then adaptive placement and geometry-aware interpolation. Add a world cache for far queries, then depth-aware interpolation. Add temporal history last, after a history-free frame is interpretable. Finally add dedicated glossy tracing and the roughness transition. This order leaves a working comparison at each change.

For each persistent resource, answer the same implementation questions: who allocates it, who initializes it, what quantity it stores, how indices map to geometry or directions, which bits indicate validity, which pass writes the current version, which consumers read it, which event invalidates it, and what happens when its budget is exhausted. Omitting one of these can produce an image that looks correct only while the camera is stationary.

The engine details are numerous because these contracts interact; the transport equation stays fixed. A new optimization should state which contract it replaces and what error it introduces, so its result can be compared with the reference path tracer it approximates.

15Testing lighting predictions in Sponza

An overly bright cache can hide excessive occlusion. Exposure can hide an indirect contribution that is missing altogether. To test one effect in Sponza, keep the saved camera, lens, materials, lights and display transform fixed. Change one mechanism and predict what should change in the capture.

Separate a finite reference from an exact answer

The path-traced images estimate the same scene with a different algorithm. A 1,024-sample image still contains sampling error, and an eight-bounce limit omits longer paths. More samples reduce sampling error for the chosen path depth, material model and atmosphere settings. Differences in any of those choices can persist at convergence. Comparing the 256- and 1,024-sample results helps identify residual reference noise. If the larger accumulation reuses the smaller one’s samples, their errors are correlated. An independent confidence interval requires independent measurements.

For a pixel or receiver region, distinguish the quantity being compared. A scene-linear radiance difference measures a lighting discrepancy under the engine's stated RGB calibration. A difference between the published PNG values measures a discrepancy after exposure, tone mapping, and display encoding. Both can be useful, but they answer different questions. A highlight compressed by the tone mapper can produce a small PNG difference even when the linear difference is large.

Use the same scale for both sides of a comparison. For an error image, state its sign convention, channel combination, and display range. A per-image minimum/maximum stretch destroys the meaning of a brightness comparison. For a diagnostic atlas, a separately declared logarithmic or false-color transform can reveal structure, provided a reader can recover the original value, validity, and address. Verify the camera invocation from the capture metadata even when the resource decodes and previews correctly.

Predict the result of each controlled change

Disable final gathering. Compare directly illuminated stone with the shaded arcade. The primary analytic-light and shadow calculation should remain identifiable while the diffuse interreflection term changes. Dedicated scene reflections and analytic specular highlights have separate controls. The control removes both diffuse GI and probe-based rough specular, so both signals contribute to the image difference. In composition, inspect which reflection contributions survive on a shiny object after the selected pass is disabled.

The control sets r.Lumen.ScreenProbeGather=0 while retaining the Lumen GI pipeline and dedicated reflections. In this implementation, that branch returns black diffuse textures and a cleared rough-specular texture. Disabling r.Lumen.DiffuseIndirect.Allow instead can select a different lighting path, including a different treatment of sky illumination; its result cannot be interpreted as subtracting one positive term from the baseline. Before interpreting a console-variable comparison, inspect the source boundary the variable controls.

Disable screen traces. Newly exposed world-trace and cache behavior should agree where both representations have adequate geometry, material, and lighting support. Differences near a silhouette or an off-screen reflector point to a representation or validity decision. A screen hit and a world hit may obtain lighting from different sources. The comparison changes both the intersection route and potentially the shading at the hit. Follow the trace route before assigning the discrepancy to one subsystem.

Change reflection routing while retaining material roughness. Changing the dedicated-reflection threshold tests which estimator supplies the response. Changing roughness at the same time changes the physical scattering problem and confounds that test. Similarly, compare cache shading and hit lighting with the same geometry and camera: material evaluation, directional shading, and cached illumination can differ even when both routes intersect the same triangle. Use the records beside the reflection discussion to identify the selected branch.

Change a light while keeping the camera still. A delayed indirect response can come from surface-cache updates, world-cache updates, probe filtering, or final temporal reconstruction. Record the actual update or render-frame identity, and inspect the intermediate signal that each stage owns. Use the renderer’s update index to align screenshots with simulation steps. Image differences can shrink even when cached lighting approaches a biased solution.

Selected observation and numerical provenance

Complete sequence record

The sequence measures update latency across the combined renderer. Isolating the final temporal filter would require a separate control. The Sun also participates in the captured sky environment, and multiple lighting stores can update after the change. The sequence record identifies draws 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64 and the engine frame counter for each. The capture bridge can issue several scene renders within one engine frame. Converting 64 draws to seconds requires independent timing. The separate Lumen Scene direct and indirect sequences show cached lighting. To recover primary direct light or isolate a particular path length, use a measurement specific to that quantity.

Read an error in the order the computation produced it

Start with the camera and primary visibility: confirm the receiver's depth, normal, material, and active view rectangle. Then inspect direct-light visibility and its contribution. From there, follow the indirect query through probe owner, direction or directional cell, accepted trace route, hit or cache lookup, radiance scale, and integration weight. Finish with spatial validity and reprojected history. A wrong normal near the start can produce a convincing sequence of internally consistent later buffers, while a history failure at the end can hide correct current-frame lighting.

For a numerical walkthrough, record the full address chain. When views or versions share a resource name, match the invocation and resource version as well. Use the scene invocation, producing pass, resource version, mip/slice, stored format, row or element stride, coordinate, and validity state. Decode pre-exposure before comparing quantities from different lighting stores. When the dump omits a shader-local branch or sample choice, state which inputs the replay uses and how you chose them. Several input choices can produce the same output. Confirm the dispatched shader’s choice with an execution record if one exists.

16Reproducing the examples and finding the engine code

The small numerical experiments are independent checks of the mathematical contracts. The code is original, uses a fixed random seed where sampling is involved, and distinguishes analytic values from Monte Carlo estimates. Run python Scripts/Docs/unreal_articles/labs/lumen-course/generate.py --check to verify the published diagrams and arithmetic. Their JSON results identify the expected value and tolerance for each check. GPU performance requires a timed GPU run.

The Sponza scene and its provenance

Unreal rendered the Khronos Sponza glTF asset at revision 8f492390 after import. The input contains 103 primitives, 262,267 triangles, 25 materials, and 69 texture images. The download record preserves the source-file hashes. Upstream credits and terms are retained in the model attribution and license record; the model's listed Cryengine Limited License is distinct from the CC-BY-4.0 license on its metadocumentation. The source asset bundle comes from the pinned upstream location.

For this scene, each primitive becomes a separate static mesh with a local pivot. Recenter positions around the primitive's source bounding-box center c, preserve the glTF node scale 0.008, import the local geometry, then place the actor at 0.8(c.x, c.z, c.y) centimetres. Unreal's metre-to-centimetre conversion and the node scale give local positions 0.8(p − c), with the same axis swap. Adding the actor translation recovers 0.8p. This keeps the original world geometry while giving each mesh a useful local domain for distance fields and cards. Reusing the original indices, UVs, normals, tangents, and material associations is essential; recreating only the silhouette would change the transport problem. These imported static meshes have Nanite disabled. Comparing Nanite fallback with native ray-tracing geometry would require a different setup.

The saved map is /Game/Labs/SponzaTeaching. The chart added to the map uses six spheres of radius 22 cm, centered at z=60 cm on 40 cm pedestals at x=850 cm. Its three roughness values are 0.08, 0.30, and 0.65, used for both a dielectric and a gold-colored metal. This gives narrow and broad scattering responses without changing the atrium's architecture.

Inspecting the captured frame

The scene-based temporal controls beside cards and radiosity, screen probes, and the world-cache discussion use thirteen additional native observations. They retain the captured camera transforms, resource versions, signed SH coefficients, allocation identities, and update counters. The temporal archive and decoder instructions preserve all 23,923 files in those selected-resource dumps: 27,141,983,250 native bytes stored in a 1,957,882,466-byte lossless package. Each visual uses its matching native screenshot and computes placement from the accompanying scene data.

The screen-probe, card/world-cache, and radiosity decoders retain their complete numerical arrays beside the lightweight figures. The independent screen-SH check compares 298,998 published coefficients with their native payloads, with no difference beyond the declared six-decimal publication rounding. The controls show the recorded update indices. Read each frame number within its own capture sequence. Synchronizing two runs requires a shared event.

Open the Sponza frame explorer to follow the actual resource versions used by this course. Start with the presented scene invocation, graph index 3, then choose the pass named beside the numerical example. A resource selection exposes formats, extent, mip/slice, addressing, producer and consumer links, captured parameters, raw channels, packed fields, and the payload's verification identity. Select the chunks for the resources you want to inspect. The full reconstruction would require 95 GB.

The data directory and reproduction instructions preserve every available capture file. SHA-256 deduplication and gzip reduce the 95,161,036,158 payload bytes to a complete 657,904,432-byte package including metadata. Independent reconstruction compared all 11,446 payloads and 1,012 native copies against their sources with zero mismatches. The package preserves every byte the dump exported. Shader-local values outside that export remain unavailable.

There are no per-pass draw counts. Eighty parameterless passes and three ShaderPrint passes lack native binding blocks. For 1,297 buffer versions, bytes exist without a matching readback-completion record; their identity at the owning pass is therefore unproved. Native uniform traversal records graph construction. A uniform’s execution-time value may require a later observation. Nine ray-tracing scene-buffer descriptors carry a staging-copy warning. Exclude them when looking for usable acceleration structures. Shader-local values and unrecorded random choices require a declared replay or additional instrumentation. Each of these limits appears in the coverage ledger.

The numerical examples preserve the distinction between captured values and replayed operations. The source/version/address chain is recorded for every sampled operand. A replay can validate arithmetic or a representation against an output, but it cannot retroactively record an unobserved thread-local branch. The original capture analysis is retained alongside a documented correction to two packed-view matrix labels. The receiver reconstruction uses the corrected layout.

The capture and decoder sources preserve the import, authoring, final configuration, controlled captures, and CPU replay logic. Capture scripts record this workstation's bridge and paths. To reproduce on another installation, supply the engine/project paths, import the pinned source asset, apply the saved rendering configuration, verify the active camera and sample-index readbacks, and only then compare results. Use the captured final configuration to check which authoring defaults were active. The package can be decoded without rerunning Unreal.

The implementation reference preserves the controlled-room experiment and its complete available resource package. Its frame explorer exposes pass/resource identities, versions, formats, extents, subresources, stored-format channels, packed bits, producer/consumer relationships, and captured parameters. Its coverage records identify missing semantic information and limits on proving native-resource timing. A raw capture cannot reveal an unrecorded shader-local intermediate; you must replay that value from recorded inputs or capture it with additional instrumentation. A preview image never substitutes for the underlying validity and addressing data.

The course's source-range record freezes the exact linked shader and C++ ranges with line-normalized SHA-256 hashes. These linked files were unchanged relative to the stated engine base commit when inspected. The capture uses a local instrumented build; its own manifest records the executable and module identities. These are separate facts: source lineage, compiled binary identity, and captured runtime settings.

The teaching order takes inspiration from Physically Based Rendering, fourth edition and Real-Time Rendering, fourth edition: connect an observable problem to a model, make the model executable, then test the consequence of changing the implementation. The prose, diagrams, and numerical examples here are original. For rigorous light-to-sensor path notation and mixed-measure sampling, continue with Eric Veach's thesis. For the production implementation, use the pinned Unreal source links beside each mechanism; newer engine revisions can change layouts, defaults, and mode selection.

This study uses Unreal 5.8.1 at commit 71fe36aac5a8. Captions identify older screenshots and presentations. You need access to Epic’s Unreal Engine repository to open the source links.
